—— 我明白。雇主喜欢对组织感兴趣的求职者，对吧？
—— 如果你能在面试中流畅地运用这类回答，一定能留下好印象。

题目

1. 这位女士的主要两难是什么？
2. 这位男士夏天很想做什么？
3. 这位男士为什么需要钱？
4. 关于工程学院我们知道什么？
5. 当被问到「工作中什么对她重要」时，建议这位女士提到什么？
6. 这位女士面试中最大的问题是什么？
7. 谈到以往经历时，这位男士提醒不要做什么？
8. 这位女士为什么应该事先准备好至少一个问题？

title: Test 5 · 长对话
en:
Conversation One

— Good morning, class.
— Good morning, sir.
— Today we'll discuss volcanoes. Can you tell me the most dangerous thing about a volcano?
— I think the most dangerous hazard of a volcano comes from the lava that flows out of it.
— Good guess. Although your answer makes sense, the biggest killer from a volcano comes from the ash, not the lava. In fact, ash causes serious problems and can make humans and animals sick. It can even kill them. Ash also reduces sunlight and can start heavy rainfalls that lead to mudslides. Did you know that it only takes 30 centimeters of dry ash to collapse a roof of a building? Ash also contaminates water supplies and kills crops. As you can see, ash causes the most destruction.
— Professor, are there different sizes of volcanoes?
— Absolutely. There are ordinary volcanoes that can kill thousands of people and often destroy whole cities, and there are super volcanoes which are highly explosive and can kill billions of people and even destroy an entire continent.
— Are there any super volcanoes in the world today?
— Actually, yes. There are 40 super volcanoes. One is in Yellowstone National Park in the United States and two others in Britain. Super volcanoes are quite rare, with the last eruption occurring about 74,000 years ago in Indonesia.
— How do super volcanoes differ from ordinary volcanoes, and are they easy to find?
— By and large, most people would not be able to recognize a super volcano. Like an iceberg, the larger part of the volcano is hidden.
— Professor, if the volcano hasn't erupted, then how do scientists know what might happen?
— Well, the scientists are relying on past information from the volcano that erupted in Indonesia, and they also forecast their predictions using computer models.

Conversation Two

— Excuse me, could you please tell me how to get to the tennis courts?
— They are right next to the sports complex.
— I am new to the university and I don't know where the sports complex is either.
— Well, it's about a five-minute walk. Head down this main road for two blocks. Turn right at the clock tower and you will be on Butte Avenue. Walk on Butte for a couple of blocks, maybe three blocks.
— You already have me walking about five blocks. Are you sure it is only a five-minute walk?
— Maybe it is longer? Actually, it could be more like 10 minutes, I am not sure.
— Do you know if there is a bus stop there?
— Yes, the bus stop is in front of the pool, but bus service is quite slow during the day.
— Are the tennis courts in good condition?
— Yes, this university is very lucky to have such sports facilities.
— That's what I've heard. Did a rich person donate some money?
— Yes, about five or six years ago. The rumor is that a famous hockey player left millions of dollars to build a new sports complex. It was an anonymous donation. Actually, I'm sorry to say I almost never used it. After my first year, besides studying, I took up cards. I love playing bridge.
— Well, I hope to get in good shape here. I'm meeting a friend at the tennis courts in 15 minutes, so I'd better be going.
— Yes, you should. Now that I think about it, it may be close to a 20-minute walk to get there.

Questions

1. What is the most dangerous thing about a volcano?
2. Where did the last eruption of a super volcano occur?
3. Why are super volcanoes not easy to find?
4. How can scientists predict the future of volcanoes?
5. What can be inferred about the woman?
6. How did the university probably obtain the new sports facilities?
7. What is the woman's favorite game?
8. What is the man trying to do?
zh:
对话一

—— 早上好，同学们。
—— 早上好，老师。
—— 今天我们讲火山。谁能告诉我，火山最危险的地方是什么？
—— 我认为火山最危险的地方是喷出来的熔岩。
—— 猜得不错。虽然你的回答说得通，但火山造成死亡最多的其实是火山灰，不是熔岩。事实上，火山灰会造成严重问题，能让人和动物生病，甚至致死。火山灰还会遮挡阳光，引发强降雨，进而导致泥石流。你们知道吗，只要 30 厘米厚的干火山灰就能压塌一栋楼的屋顶。火山灰还会污染水源、毁坏庄稼。如你所见，火山灰造成的破坏最大。
—— 教授，火山有大小之分吗？
—— 当然。有普通火山，能杀死数千人，常常摧毁整座城市；还有超级火山，爆炸性极强，能杀死数十亿人，甚至摧毁整块大陆。
—— 今天世界上还有超级火山吗？
—— 其实有。世界上有 40 座超级火山，一座在美国黄石国家公园，另外两座在英国。超级火山相当罕见，最后一次喷发大约是 7.4 万年前在印度尼西亚。
—— 超级火山和普通火山有什么不同？它们容易发现吗？
—— 总的来说，大多数人根本认不出超级火山。就像冰山一样，火山更大的一部分是隐藏着的。
—— 教授，如果火山还没喷发，科学家怎么知道可能会发生什么？
—— 科学家依靠印度尼西亚那次喷发留下的历史资料，同时也用计算机模型来做预测。

对话二

—— 打扰一下，能告诉我网球场怎么走吗？
—— 就在综合体育馆旁边。
—— 我刚来这所大学，我也不知道综合体育馆在哪儿。
—— 嗯，走过去大概五分钟。沿这条主路走两个街区，在钟楼那儿右转，就到比特大道了。在比特大道上走两三个街区。
—— 你这一说我已经走了五个街区了。你确定只要五分钟？
—— 也许更久？其实更可能是 10 分钟，我也不太确定。
—— 你知道那儿有公交站吗？
—— 有，公交站在游泳池前面，不过白天的班次很慢。
—— 网球场条件好吗？
—— 好，这所大学能有这样的体育设施真是很幸运。
—— 我也听说过。是有钱人捐的吗？
—— 是的，大概五六年前。传闻是一位有名的冰球运动员留下几百万美元建了新的综合体育馆，是匿名捐赠。说起来很惭愧，我几乎没用过。大一之后，除了学习，我玩起了牌，我很喜欢打桥牌。
—— 嗯，我希望在这儿把身体练好。我 15 分钟后约了朋友在网球场见，得走了。
—— 是该走了。现在想想，走到那儿可能接近 20 分钟。

title: Test 6 · 长对话
en:
Conversation One

— Good evening and welcome to tonight's edition of Legendary Lives. Our subject this evening is James Dean, actor and hero for the young people of his time. Edward Murray is the author of a new biography of Dean. Good evening, Edward.
— Hello, Tina.
— Edward, tell us what you know about Dean's early life.
— He was born in Indiana in 1931, but his parents moved to California when he was five. He wasn't there long, though, because his mother passed away just four years later. Jimmy's father sent him back to Indiana after that to live with his aunt.
— So how did he get into acting?
— Well, first he acted in plays at high school. Then he went to college in California, where he got seriously into acting. In 1951 he moved to New York to do more stage acting.
— Then when did his movie career really start?
— 1955. His first starring role was in East of Eden. It was fabulous. Dean became a huge success. But the movie that really made him famous was his second one, Rebel Without a Cause. That was about teenagers who felt like they didn't fit into society.
— So how many more movies did he make?
— Just one more. Then he died in that car crash in California in 1955.
— What a tragedy. He only made three movies. So what made him the legend he still is today?
— Well, I guess his looks, his acting ability, his short life. And maybe the type of character he played in his movies. Many young people saw him as a symbol of American youth.

Conversation Two

— Mr. Stern, may I ask you, do you think it was necessary and fair to arrest Steve Brill?
— I don't know whether you realize that this man has been eating up our park for five years, and he is encouraging other people to do the same thing every single day. He's been organizing groups to destroy our urban wildlife.
— But Mr. Stern, this situation has been going on happily for five years. Why do you suddenly decide to do something about it?
— Well, at first we just thought he was an eccentric person, a bit odd, you know. But over the years we came to realize that he is a dangerous guy. He's been ruining our city environment. Parks are to look at, not to eat. It's just as if you're going to allow people to walk through a zoo and eat the baby bears.
— But surely you or your park keepers, Mr. Stern, could have discouraged Mr. Brill from his activity without going such drastic measures — without arresting him.
— Steve is a nice fellow, but what he is doing is illegal. He knows an awful lot about wild weeds. We'll be very happy to let him organize tours if he just wouldn't eat the plants and wouldn't encourage other people to do so too. You never know what this could lead to — all sorts of people ruining our park in all sorts of ways. This kind of thing is very definitely criminal behavior and must be stopped.

Questions

1. What is the woman doing?
2. Why did James Dean move back to Indiana when he was young?
3. What does the man say James Dean did at college in California?
4. What do we learn about James Dean from the conversation?
5. What does the man say Steve Brill has been doing?
6. Why was Steve Brill not arrested years ago?
7. What does the woman think of the action taken against Steve Brill?
8. What finally led to Steve Brill's arrest?
zh:
对话一

—— 晚上好，欢迎收看今晚的《传奇人生》。今晚的主角是詹姆斯·迪恩——演员，也是他那个时代年轻人的偶像。爱德华·默里是迪恩新传记的作者。晚上好，爱德华。
—— 你好，蒂娜。
—— 爱德华，给我们讲讲迪恩的早年生活吧。
—— 他 1931 年出生在印第安纳州，但五岁时父母搬到了加利福尼亚。不过他在那儿没待多久，因为仅仅四年后他母亲就去世了。之后吉米的父亲把他送回印第安纳，跟姑妈一起生活。
—— 那他是怎么进入演艺圈的？
—— 他先是在高中演话剧，后来去加州上大学，在那儿真正迷上了表演。1951 年他搬到纽约，演更多舞台剧。
—— 那他的电影生涯是什么时候真正开始的？
—— 1955 年。他的第一个主演角色是《伊甸园之东》，简直太精彩了，迪恩一炮而红。但真正让他出名的是第二部电影《无因的反叛》，讲的是那些觉得自己不被社会接纳的青少年。
—— 那他一共演了多少部电影？
—— 只多演了一部。然后在 1955 年，他死于加州的那场车祸。
—— 太可惜了，他只演了三部电影。那是什么让他至今仍是传奇？
—— 我想是他的外貌、他的演技、他短暂的一生，也许还有他在电影里扮演的那类角色。许多年轻人把他看作美国青年的象征。

对话二

—— 斯特恩先生，我能问一下吗？您认为逮捕史蒂夫·布里尔是必要且公正的吗？
—— 我不知道你有没有意识到，这个人五年来一直在「吃」我们的公园，而且每天都在鼓励别人也这么干。他一直组织人群破坏我们城市的野生植物。
—— 可是斯特恩先生，这种情况已经「愉快地」持续了五年。为什么您突然决定要处理它？
—— 嗯，一开始我们只当他是个古怪的人，有点怪，你知道的。但这几年下来，我们意识到他是个危险的家伙。他一直在毁坏我们的城市环境。公园是用来看的，不是用来吃的。这就好比你允许人们穿过动物园去吃小熊。
—— 但斯特恩先生，您或您的公园管理员总可以不采取这么激烈的手段——不用逮捕他——就劝阻布里尔先生吧。
—— 史蒂夫是个好人，但他做的事是违法的。他对野生杂草了解得非常多。只要他不吃那些植物、也不鼓励别人这么做，我们很乐意让他组织导览。你永远不知道这会发展成什么样——各种人以各种方式毁掉我们的公园。这种事绝对是犯罪行为，必须制止。

题目

1. 这位女士在做什么？
2. 詹姆斯·迪恩小时候为什么搬回印第安纳州？
3. 这位男士说詹姆斯·迪恩在加州上大学时做了什么？
4. 从对话中我们了解到詹姆斯·迪恩的什么？
5. 这位男士说史蒂夫·布里尔一直在做什么？
6. 史蒂夫·布里尔为什么多年前没有被逮捕？
7. 这位女士如何看待对史蒂夫·布里尔采取的行动？
8. 最终是什么导致史蒂夫·布里尔被捕？

title: Test 7 · 长对话
en:
Conversation One

— Can we make you an offer? We would like to run the campaign for four extra weeks.
— Well, can we summarize the problem from our point of view? First of all, the campaign was late — it missed two important trade fairs. The ads also did not appear in two key magazines. As a result, the campaign failed. Do you accept that summary of what happened?
— Well, the delay wasn't entirely our fault. You did in fact make late changes to the specifications of the advertisements.
— Hmm, actually, you were late with the initial proposals, so we had very little time. And in fact we only asked for small changes.
— Well, whatever. Can we repeat our offer to run the campaign for four extra weeks?
— That's not really the point. The campaign missed two key trade fairs. Because of this, we're asking you either to repeat the campaign next year for free, or we only pay 50% of the fee for this year.
— Could we suggest a 20% reduction to the fee, together with a four-week extension to the campaign?
— We are not happy. We lost business.
— I think we both made mistakes. The responsibility is on both sides.
— Okay, let's suggest a new solution. How about a 40% cut in fee, or a free repeat campaign?
— Well, let's take a break. We're not getting very far. Perhaps we should think about this.

Conversation Two

— You know, I've often wondered why people laugh at a picture of a big-bellied businessman slipping on a banana skin and falling on his bottom.
— We like to feel sorry for him.
— Actually, Laura, I think we laugh because we're glad it didn't happen to us. But of course, there's also a kind of humorous satisfaction in seeing somebody self-important making a fool of themselves.
— Yes. And then there are a lot of jokes about people who are too fat or physically handicapped — you know, deaf or short-sighted, things like that. After all, it's not really funny to be like that.
— Oh, I think that's because we're embarrassed. We don't know how to cope with the situation. Perhaps we are even a bit frightened we might get like that, so we laugh.
— What about the custard pie routine?
— What do you mean, custard pie routine?
— Oh, you know, all those old films where somebody gets so outraged with his boss, he picks up a custard pie and plasters it all over the other person's face?
— That never makes me laugh very much, because you can guess it's going to happen. But a lot of people still find it laughable. It must be because it's the sort of thing we'd all love to do once in a while and never quite have the courage to.
— I had an old aunt who used to throw cups of tea at people when she was particularly irritated. She said it relieved her feelings.
— It must have come a bit expensive.
— Not really. She took care never to throw her best china.

Questions

1. What do we learn about the man's company?
2. Why was the campaign delayed, according to the man?
3. What did the woman propose as a solution to the problem?
4. What does the man suggest they do at the end of the conversation?
5. Why does the man say we laugh when we see some self-important people making fools of themselves?
6. Why do some people joke about those who are fat or handicapped, according to the man?
7. Why do many people find it funny to see someone throwing a custard pie at their boss's face?
8. Why did the man's aunt say she would throw cups of tea at people occasionally?
zh:
对话一

—— 我们能给你一个方案吗？我们希望把这次广告活动再延长四周。
—— 那么，我们能不能从我们的角度归纳一下问题？首先，这次活动做晚了，错过了两个重要的交易会。广告也没有在两本关键杂志上刊登。结果，活动失败了。你接受这个说法吗？
—— 嗯，延期并不完全是我们的错。事实上，你们后来对广告规格做了改动，而且改得很晚。
—— 唔，其实你们最初的方案就交晚了，所以我们时间很少；而且事实上我们只要求了很小的改动。
—— 好吧，随便怎么说。我们能不能重复一下方案：把活动延长四周？
—— 这不是重点。活动错过了两个关键交易会。因此，我们要求：要么明年免费重做一次活动，要么今年的费用我们只付 50%。
—— 我们能不能提议费用减 20%，活动延长四周？
—— 我们不满意，我们丢了生意。
—— 我认为双方都有错，责任在双方。
—— 好吧，那我们提个新方案：费用减 40%，或者免费重做一次活动，怎么样？
—— 这样吧，我们休息一下。现在谈不出什么结果，也许我们该再想想。

对话二

—— 你知道吗，我常常纳闷：为什么人们看到一张大肚子商人踩到香蕉皮、一屁股摔在地上的照片就会笑？
—— 我们会替他感到难过吧。
—— 其实，劳拉，我觉得我们笑是因为庆幸这事没发生在自己身上。当然，看到一个自以为了不起的人出丑，也会有一种幽默的满足感。
—— 是的。还有很多笑话是关于太胖的人或身体有残障的人——比如聋人、近视的人之类的。毕竟，那样本身并不真的好笑。
—— 哦，我觉得那是因为我们尴尬，不知道该怎么应对这种场面。也许我们还隐隐害怕自己会变成那样，所以就笑了。
—— 那「奶油派」那一套呢？
—— 你说「奶油派」那一套是什么意思？
—— 哦，你知道的，就是那些老电影里，某个人被老板气得不行，抓起一个奶油派就往对方脸上抹。
—— 那从来不太能让我笑，因为你能猜到它一定会发生。但很多人还是觉得好笑。一定是因为那是我们偶尔都想干、却又始终没那个胆量去干的事。
—— 我有个老姑妈，特别恼火的时候就朝人扔茶杯。她说这样能发泄情绪。
—— 那代价恐怕有点高吧。
—— 也不见得，她从来很小心的，绝不扔她最好的瓷器。

题目

1. 关于这位男士的公司，我们了解到什么？
2. 按这位男士的说法，广告活动为什么延期？
3. 这位女士提出了什么解决方案？
4. 对话最后这位男士建议他们做什么？
5. 这位男士为什么说，我们看到那些自以为了不起的人出丑时会笑？
6. 按这位男士的说法，为什么有些人会拿胖子或残障人士开玩笑？
7. 为什么很多人觉得看到别人往老板脸上扔奶油派很好笑？
8. 这位男士的姑妈为什么说她偶尔会朝人扔茶杯？

title: Test 8 · 长对话
en:
Conversation One

— There is an element there about competition though, isn't there? Because British Railways is a nationalized industry, there's only one railway system in the country. If you don't like a particular can of baked beans, you can go and buy another, but if you don't like a particular railway, you can't go and use another.
— Some people who write to me say this. They say that if you didn't have a monopoly, you wouldn't be able to do the things you do.
— Well, I don't think we do anything deliberately to upset our customers. We have particular problems. Since 1946, when the Transport Act came in, we were nationalized.
— Do you think that is a good thing? Has it been a good thing for the railways, do you think, to be nationalized?
— Oh, I think so, yes. Because in general, modes of transport are all around. Let's face the fact: the car arrived, the car is here to stay, there is no question about that.
— So what you're saying then is that if the railways hadn't been nationalized, they would simply have disappeared.
— Oh, I think they would have. They're disappearing fast in America. The French railways lose 1 billion pounds a year; the German railways, 2 billion pounds a year. But you see, those governments are prepared to pour money into the transport system to keep it going.
— So in a sense, you cope between two extremes. On the one hand, you're trying not to lose too much money, and on the other hand, you've got to provide the best service.
— Yes, you're right.

Conversation Two

— I see on your new resume that you worked as a manager of a store called Computer Country. Could you tell me a little more about your responsibilities there?
— Sure. I was responsible for overseeing about 30 employees. I did all of the ordering for the store, and I kept track of the inventory.
— What was the most difficult part of your job?
— Probably handling angry customers. We didn't have them very often, but when we did, I needed to make sure they were well taken care of. After all, the customer is always right.
— That's how we feel here too. How long did you work there?
— I was there for three and a half years. I left the company last month.
— And why did you leave?
— My husband has been transferred to Boston, and I understand your company has an opening there too.
— Yes, that's right, we do. But the position won't start until early next month. Would that be a problem for you?
— No, not at all. My husband's new job doesn't begin for a few weeks, so we thought we would spend some time driving to Boston and stop to see my parents.
— That sounds nice. So tell me, why are you interested in this particular position?
— I know that your company has a great reputation and a wonderful product. I've thought many times that I would like to be a part of it. When I heard about the opening in Boston, I jumped at the opportunity.
— Well, I'm glad you did.

Questions

1. What does the woman say about British Railways?
2. What do some people who write to the man complain about?
3. What does the man say threatens the existence of railways?
4. What does the man say about railways in other countries?
5. What was the woman's previous job?
6. What does the woman say was the most difficult part of her job?
7. Why is the woman looking for a job in Boston?
8. When can the woman start to work if she gets the job?
zh:
对话一

—— 不过这里有个竞争的问题，对吧？因为英国铁路是国有企业，全国只有一个铁路系统。如果你不喜欢某个牌子的焗豆，你可以去买别的；但如果你不喜欢某条铁路，你没别的可用啊。
—— 有些给我写信的人就是这么说的。他们说，如果没有垄断，你们根本做不成现在做的这些事。
—— 嗯，我认为我们并没有故意去让乘客不满。我们有特殊的难题：自 1946 年《运输法》出台，我们就被国有化了。
—— 你觉得那是好事吗？你认为对铁路来说，国有化是件好事吗？
—— 哦，我认为是的。因为总的说来，各种交通方式都摆在眼前。我们面对现实吧：汽车出现了，汽车会留下来，这一点毫无疑问。
—— 那么你的意思是，如果铁路没有被国有化，它们就干脆消失了。
—— 哦，我想会的。它们在美国正迅速消失。法国铁路一年亏 10 亿英镑，德国铁路一年亏 20 亿英镑。可你看，那些政府愿意往交通系统里投钱，让它维持下去。
—— 所以某种意义上说，你在两个极端之间周旋：一方面尽量别亏太多钱，另一方面还得提供最好的服务。
—— 是的，你说得对。

对话二

—— 我看到你的新简历上写着，你曾在一家叫「电脑国度」的商店当经理。能多讲讲你在那儿的职责吗？
—— 当然。我负责管理大约 30 名员工，店里所有的订货都由我做，我还负责跟踪库存。
—— 你工作中最难的部分是什么？
—— 大概是应付生气的顾客。这种顾客不常有，但一旦有，我就得确保他们得到妥善照顾。毕竟，顾客永远是对的。
—— 我们这儿也是这么想的。你在那儿工作了多久？
—— 三年半。我上个月离职了。
—— 那为什么离职？
—— 我丈夫被调到波士顿，我了解到贵公司在那边也有一个空缺。
—— 对，没错，我们有。但这个职位要到下月初才开始。这对你有问题吗？
—— 完全没有。我丈夫的新工作还要过几周才开始，所以我们打算开车去波士顿，路上顺便看看我父母。
—— 听起来不错。那告诉我，你为什么对这个职位感兴趣？
—— 我知道贵公司声誉很好，产品也很棒。我好多次都想，希望能成为其中一员。听说波士顿有空缺时，我立刻就抓住了这个机会。
—— 我很高兴你这么做。

题目

1. 这位女士对英国铁路说了什么？
2. 给这位男士写信的那些人在抱怨什么？
3. 这位男士说是什么威胁着铁路的生存？
4. 这位男士对别国的铁路说了什么？
5. 这位女士以前的工作是什么？
6. 这位女士说她工作中最难的部分是什么？
7. 这位女士为什么要在波士顿找工作？
8. 如果她得到这份工作，什么时候能上班？

title: Test 9 · 长对话
en:
Conversation One

— Well, in the studio this morning for our interview spot is Peter Wilson. Peter works for Greenpeace. So Peter, welcome.
— Thanks a lot. It's good to be here.
— Now Peter, perhaps you could tell us something about Greenpeace and your job there?
— Sure. Well, I'll start by telling you roughly what Greenpeace is all about. I actually work in London for the Greenpeace organization. We've been going for a few decades and we're a nonviolent, nonpolitical organization. We're involved in anti-nuclear activity, conservation and protection of animals, and protection and support of our ecosystem. I'm the action organizer and arrange any protests.
— A pretty important role. Peter, what sort of protests would you organize?
— Well, recently we've been involved in anti-nuclear campaigns. I personally arranged for the demonstration against radioactive waste dumping in the Atlantic Ocean. We've got a few small Greenpeace boats that we harass the dumping ships with.
— Hold on, Peter. I thought you said your organization was nonviolent. What do you mean by "harass"?
— Well, we circle round and round the ships and get in the way when they try to dump the drums of nuclear waste in the sea. We talk to the men and try to change — you know, yell at them to stop. We generally make ourselves as much of a nuisance as possible.
— Well, people may think differently of your methods, but there's no doubt you're doing a great job. Keep it up and good luck, and thanks for talking with us.
— Thanks for having me.

Conversation Two

— Tell me, Peter, what makes Harrods so famous?
— Well, it's the biggest department store in the UK, and its food hall and Egyptian hall are very famous. People come to Harrods just to see them.
— What is special about the food hall?
— It sells many different kinds of food. For example, it has 250 kinds of cheese from all over the world and more than 180 kinds of bread. Customers also love all the different kinds of chocolate. They buy a hundred tons every year.
— That's amazing. And why is the Egyptian hall so famous?
— Well, when people see it, they feel they're in another world. It looks like an Egyptian building from 4,000 years ago, and it sells beautiful objects. They are not 4,000 years old, of course.
— Is it true that Harrods produces its own electricity?
— Yes, it does — 70%, enough for a small town — to light the outside of the building. We use 11,500 light bulbs.
— Really. Tell me, how many customers do you have on an average day, and how much do they spend?
— About 30,000 people come on an average day. But during the sales, the number increases to 300,000 customers a day.
— How much do they spend?
— Well, on average, customers spend about 1.5 million pounds a day. The record for one day is 9 million pounds.
— 9 million pounds in one day?
— Yes, on the first day of the January sales.
— Harrods says it sells everything to everybody everywhere. Is that really true?
— Oh, yes, of course — absolutely everything.

Questions

1. What is the man's chief responsibility in the Greenpeace organization?
2. What has Greenpeace been involved in recently?
3. How does Greenpeace try to stop people from dumping nuclear waste?
4. What is the woman's attitude towards the Greenpeace campaigns?
5. What is the food hall of Harrods noted for?
6. What does the Egyptian hall seem like to the customers?
7. What may customers find surprising about Harrods?
8. About how many customers come to Harrods on an average day?
zh:
对话一

—— 今天上午来到我们演播室接受采访的是彼得·威尔逊。彼得在绿色和平组织工作。彼得，欢迎你。
—— 非常感谢，很高兴来这儿。
—— 彼得，能不能给我们介绍一下绿色和平组织，还有你在那里的工作？
—— 好的。我先大致讲讲绿色和平组织是干什么的。我其实是在伦敦的绿色和平组织工作。我们已经开展了几十年，是一个非暴力、非政治的组织。我们参与反核活动、自然保护与动物保护，以及生态系统的保护与支持。我是行动组织者，负责安排各种抗议活动。
—— 相当重要的角色。彼得，你会组织什么样的抗议？
—— 最近我们一直在参与反核运动。我亲自安排了反对在大西洋倾倒放射性废料的示威。我们有几艘绿色和平的小船，用来骚扰那些倾倒废料的船只。
—— 等等，彼得。我记得你说过你们组织是非暴力的。你说的「骚扰」是什么意思？
—— 我们绕着那些船一圈一圈地转，在它们想把核废料桶倒进海里时挡住去路。我们跟那些船员谈话，试图改变他们——你懂的，冲他们喊，让他们停下来。总之我们尽可能给他们制造麻烦。
—— 人们也许对你的方式有不同看法，但毫无疑问你们做得很好。继续加油，祝你们好运，谢谢你接受采访。
—— 谢谢邀请。

对话二

—— 彼得，跟我说说，哈罗德百货为什么这么有名？
—— 它是英国最大的百货商店，它的食品大厅和埃及大厅非常有名。人们专门来哈罗德就是为了看这两个大厅。
—— 食品大厅有什么特别之处？
—— 它卖很多种不同的食品。比如，它有来自世界各地 250 种奶酪，还有 180 多种面包。顾客也很喜欢各种不同的巧克力，一年要买一百吨。
—— 太惊人了。那埃及大厅为什么这么有名？
—— 人们看到它时，会觉得自己到了另一个世界。它看起来像一座 4000 年前的埃及建筑，里面卖精美的工艺品。当然，它们并不是 4000 年前的。
—— 听说哈罗德自己发电，是真的吗？
—— 是的，70% 靠自发电，够一个小镇用，用来点亮大楼外部。我们用了 11500 只灯泡。
—— 真的。那平均每天有多少顾客，他们花多少钱？
—— 平均每天大约有三万人来。但在打折期间，顾客人数会增加到每天三十万。
—— 他们花多少钱？
—— 平均来说，顾客每天花掉约 150 万英镑。单日最高纪录是 900 万英镑。
—— 一天 900 万英镑？
—— 是的，就在一月打折季的第一天。
—— 哈罗德说它「把一切卖给所有人」。这话是真的吗？
—— 哦，是的，当然——绝对是一切的。

题目

1. 这位男士在绿色和平组织中的主要职责是什么？
2. 绿色和平组织最近在参与什么？
3. 绿色和平组织如何设法阻止人们倾倒核废料？
4. 这位女士对绿色和平组织的行动持什么态度？
5. 哈罗德的食品大厅以什么著称？
6. 埃及大厅在顾客看来像什么？
7. 顾客可能对哈罗德的什么感到惊讶？
8. 平均每天大约有多少顾客到哈罗德？

title: Test 10 · 长对话
en:
Conversation One

— Hello and welcome to our program Working Abroad. Our guest this evening is a Londoner who lives and works in Italy. Her name's Susan Hill. Susan, welcome to the program. You live in Florence — how long have you been living there?
— Since 1982. But when I went there in 1982, I planned to stay for only six months.
— Why did you change your mind?
— Well, I'm a designer. I design leather goods, mainly shoes and handbags. Soon after I arrived in Florence, I got a job with one of Italy's top fashion houses, Ferragamo. So I decided to stay.
— How lucky! Do you still work for Ferragamo?
— No, I've been a freelance designer for quite a long time now — since 1988, in fact.
— So does that mean you design for several different companies now?
— Yes, that's right. I've designed many fashion items for a number of Italian companies. And in the last four years I've also been designing for the British company Burberrys.
— What have you been designing for them?
— Mostly handbags and small leather goods.
— Has the fashion industry in Italy changed since 1982?
— Oh, yes. It's become a lot more competitive, because the quality of products from other countries has improved a lot. But Italian quality and design is still world famous.
— And do you ever think of returning to live in England?
— No, not really. Working in Italy is more interesting. I also love the Mediterranean sun and the Italian lifestyle.
— Well, thank you for talking to us, Susan.
— It was a pleasure.

Conversation Two

— Hi Anne, welcome back. How was your trip to the States?
— Very busy. I had a lot of meetings, so of course I didn't have much time to see New York.
— What a pity. Actually, I have a trip there myself next week. Do you take my advice — do the "Well-being in the Air" program? It really works.
— Oh, I read about that in a magazine. You say it works?
— Yes. I did the program on the flight to the States, and when I arrived in New York, I didn't have any problem — no jet lag at all. On the way back, I didn't do it and I felt terrible.
— You're joking?
— Not at all. It really made a lot of difference.
— So what did you do?
— Well, I didn't drink any alcohol or coffee, and I didn't eat any meat or rich food. I drank a lot of water and fruit juice, and I ate the meals on the well-being menu. They're lighter — they have fish, vegetables and noodles, for example. And I did some of the exercises in the program.
— Exercises on a plane?
— Yes. I didn't do many, of course — there isn't much space on a plane.
— How many passengers did the exercises?
— Not many.
— And how much champagne did they drink?
— A lot. It was more popular than mineral water.
— So basically it's a choice: mineral water and exercises, or champagne and jet lag.
— That's right. It's a difficult choice.

Questions

1. Where does this talk most probably take place?
2. What was the woman's original plan when she went to Florence?
3. What has the woman been doing for a living since 1988?
4. What do we learn about the change in Italy's fashion industry?
5. Why did the woman go to New York?
6. What does the woman say about the "Well-being in the Air" program?
7. What did the woman do to follow the well-being menu?
8. What did the woman say about other passengers?
zh:
对话一

—— 大家好，欢迎收听我们的节目《海外工作》。今晚的嘉宾是一位在意大利生活和工作的伦敦人，她叫苏珊·希尔。苏珊，欢迎来到节目。你住在佛罗伦萨——在那儿住了多久了？
—— 从 1982 年住到现在。不过我 1982 年去的时候，原计划只待六个月。
—— 为什么改了主意？
—— 我是设计师，做皮具设计，主要是鞋和手袋。到佛罗伦萨后不久，我就进了意大利顶级时装公司之一菲拉格慕工作，于是就决定留下了。
—— 真幸运！你现在还在菲拉格慕工作吗？
—— 不在了，我做自由设计师已经很久了——其实从 1988 年就开始了。
—— 那意味着你现在为好几家不同的公司做设计？
—— 对。我为不少意大利公司设计过许多时尚单品。最近四年我还在为英国公司巴宝莉做设计。
—— 你为他们设计什么？
—— 主要是手袋和小件皮具。
—— 1982 年以来，意大利的时装业有变化吗？
—— 哦，有。竞争激烈了很多，因为其他国家的产品质量提高了很多。不过意大利的品质和设计仍然世界闻名。
—— 你有没有想过回英国生活？
—— 没有，真的没有。在意大利工作更有意思，我也喜欢地中海的阳光和意大利的生活方式。
—— 好，谢谢你接受采访，苏珊。
—— 很荣幸。

对话二

—— 嗨，安妮，欢迎回来。你这趟去美国怎么样？
—— 特别忙。会很多，所以当然没什么时间逛纽约。
—— 太可惜了。其实我下周也要去一趟。你听我的建议了吗？做那个「空中健康」项目？真的有效。
—— 哦，我在一本杂志上看到过。你说有效？
—— 有效。我在去美国的航班上做了那个项目，到纽约时一点问题都没有——完全没有时差反应。回来的时候我没做，感觉糟透了。
—— 你开玩笑吧？
—— 一点不假，差别真的很大。
—— 那你都做了什么？
—— 我没喝任何酒和咖啡，也没吃肉或油腻的食物。我喝了很多水和果汁，吃的是健康菜单上的餐食。那些比较清淡——比如有鱼、蔬菜和面条。我还做了项目里的一些体操。
—— 在飞机上做体操？
—— 对。当然我没做多少，飞机上空间不大。
—— 有多少乘客做体操？
—— 不多。
—— 那他们喝了多少香槟？
—— 很多，比矿泉水还受欢迎。
—— 所以基本上就是个选择：矿泉水和体操，或者香槟和时差。
—— 没错，这是个艰难的选择。

题目

1. 这段谈话最可能发生在哪里？
2. 这位女士去佛罗伦萨时的原计划是什么？
3. 自 1988 年以来，这位女士一直以什么为业？
4. 关于意大利时装业的变化，我们了解到什么？
5. 这位女士为什么去纽约？
6. 这位女士如何评价「空中健康」项目？
7. 这位女士为遵循健康菜单做了什么？
8. 这位女士对其他乘客说了什么？

title: Test 1 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

From California to Connecticut, babies sit on the laps of their parents or caretakers and are spoken to in Italian, French, Spanish and, increasingly, Chinese. They sit in circles, distracted by cuddly toys, at schools such as the Language Workshop in New York, or in formal groups organized by parents.

There have been several studies that have found advantages in starting children off in a new language at a young age. Researchers don't know whether it is biological or social, but most children who learn a language before puberty seem to develop the ability to speak it as a native would.

Francois, who runs the Language Workshop, has created a line of linguistic software for young children. "Understanding comes long before speaking, and speaking before reading and writing. That's the way we teach the languages," Francois says. "When we translate for children, we actually add confusion. It is not necessary in our class. For clarity, we have to repeat the word until the idea sinks in."

Some parents fear that with all these different words and languages, their children will have a harder time picking up English or will get confused. But scientists have found no such disadvantage to being multilingual. There are emerging theories that the brain is designed to pick up multiple languages early in life, and that our current monolingual focus is actually a setback of evolution. Some research shows there is a window in which children can most readily absorb new languages: for the first six months of life, for example, babies can hear every sound from every language in the world.

Passage Two

You could say that Joseph Cornell became an artist because of his love of collecting. Cornell used to spend his free time exploring the street life of New York City in the 1920s. He soon started collecting old books, prints, postcards and even three-dimensional objects that he found in stores that sold used books.

Cornell also attended many museum shows, gallery openings and dance performances. He was influenced by a group of artists called the Surrealists, who combined images in unusual and often strange ways.

Joseph Cornell started making his own works by cutting out different pictures and putting them together in creative and magical combinations. Soon he started making boxes, inside of which were carefully arranged pictures and objects. He worked on his art at night after finishing his day job. Later, when his boxes and images started selling and receiving public recognition, he worked on his art full time.

Joseph Cornell died in 1972. The Smithsonian exhibit showed almost 200 works made during his 40-year career. One work is called "Soap Bubble Set": a box with a glass window shows a map of the moon, several pictures of sea creatures, two glass cups and two white pipes for smoking. In another box, Cornell combines an image of a cockatoo bird with a music box and watch faces.

Joseph Cornell once said his art was based on everyday experiences. He said that with his art, he showed the beauty of the commonplace. Visitors who came to this special exhibit found magic in regular objects — and even saw beauty in a box.

Questions

9. What is the purpose of the Language Workshop?
10. How do the teachers in the Language Workshop teach?
11. What do the scientists think about the multilingual phenomenon?
12. What did Cornell do before making his work of art?
13. How did Cornell work on his art at the beginning?
14. How many works of Joseph Cornell were shown in the Smithsonian exhibit?
15. What can we see in his work "Soap Bubble Set"?
zh:
篇章一

从加利福尼亚到康涅狄格，婴儿们坐在父母或看护人的膝上，听人用意大利语、法语、西班牙语以及越来越多的汉语跟他们说话。在纽约「语言工作坊」这样的学校里，或者由家长组织的正式小组里，他们围坐成一圈，被毛绒玩具吸引着注意力。

已有好几项研究发现，让孩子从小接触一门新语言有好处。研究人员不清楚这是生理原因还是社会原因，但大多数在青春期之前学一门语言的孩子，似乎都能形成像母语者那样说话的能力。

经营「语言工作坊」的弗朗索瓦开发了一系列面向幼儿的语言学习软件。弗朗索瓦说：「理解远早于开口，开口又早于读写，我们就是这样教语言的。当我们为孩子翻译时，其实是在增加混乱，在我们的课上没有必要。为了讲清楚，我们要重复那个词，直到这个概念真正被吸收。」

有些家长担心，这么多不同的词和语言会让孩子更难学会英语，或者把他们弄糊涂。但科学家并没有发现多语种会带来这样的劣势。正在形成的一些理论认为，大脑天生就适合在生命早期习得多种语言，而我们目前只重视单一语言，其实是进化的倒退。一些研究显示，存在一个孩子最容易吸收新语言的「窗口期」：例如在出生后的头六个月，婴儿能听出世界上每种语言里的每一个音。

篇章二

可以说，约瑟夫·康奈尔成为艺术家，是因为他热爱收藏。20 世纪 20 年代，康奈尔常把空闲时间用来逛纽约的街头生活。他很快就开始收集旧书、版画、明信片，甚至从卖旧书的店里找到的立体物件。

康奈尔还参加了很多博物馆展览、画廊开幕和舞蹈演出。他受到一群被称为「超现实主义者」的艺术家的影响，这些人以不寻常、常常很奇怪的方式组合图像。

约瑟夫·康奈尔开始创作自己的作品：他把不同的图片剪下来，用富有创意而神奇的组合方式拼在一起。不久他开始做盒子，盒子里精心摆放着图片和物件。他白天上完班，晚上做艺术。后来，当他的盒子和图像开始卖得出去、并获得公众认可时，他就全职做艺术了。

约瑟夫·康奈尔于 1972 年去世。史密森尼的展览展出了他 40 年职业生涯中创作的近 200 件作品。其中一件叫《肥皂泡套装》：一个有玻璃窗的盒子里，展示着一幅月球地图、几张海洋生物图片、两个玻璃杯和两支白色烟斗。在另一个盒子里，康奈尔把一只凤头鹦鹉的图像和八音盒、表盘组合在一起。

约瑟夫·康奈尔曾说，他的艺术建立在日常经验之上。他说，他用自己的艺术展现了平凡事物的美。来参观这个特别展览的人，在寻常物件中发现了魔力——甚至在一个盒子里看到了美。

题目

9. 「语言工作坊」的目的是什么？
10. 「语言工作坊」的老师怎么教？
11. 科学家如何看待多语现象？
12. 康奈尔在做艺术作品之前做什么？
13. 康奈尔起初是怎样做艺术的？
14. 史密森尼展览展出了约瑟夫·康奈尔多少件作品？
15. 在他的作品《肥皂泡套装》里我们能看见什么？

title: Test 2 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

A sophomore at Colorado State University first had a problem in taking tests when she began college. She said that she was well prepared for her tests. Sometimes she studied for weeks before a test, yet she would go in to take the test only to find she could not answer the questions correctly. She would blank out because of nervousness and fear. She couldn't think of the answer. Her low grades made her teachers surprised.

In fact, what the student was experiencing is called test anxiety. Because the student worries and is uneasy about a test, her mind does not work as well as it usually does. The student cannot write or think clearly because of extreme tension and nervousness.

Although poor grades are often a result of poor study habits, sometimes test anxiety causes the low grades. Recently, test anxiety has been recognized as a real problem, not just an excuse or a false explanation of lazy students.

There are some special counseling courses in universities trying to help students with the same problem. In these courses, counselors try to help students by teaching them how to manage test anxiety. At some universities, students are asked to take tests to measure their anxiety. If the tests show that their anxiety level is high, the students will take short courses to help them deal with their tension. These courses teach students how to relax their bodies. Students are trained to become calm in very tense situations. By controlling their nervousness, they can let their minds work easily, and their learned information then comes out without difficulty on a test.

Passage Two

Recently, a five-year study was conducted by the Center for Childhood Development in Los Angeles, California, regarding the way babies react to different types of people. The findings of the study suggest that infant children seem to be more comfortable around other babies than they are with strange adults.

The results confirm the ideas of Doctor Richard Perlman, who has written many books about raising children. Dr. Perlman supports the findings of the study and adds that it is a sounder idea to keep children with other children, as in a daycare center, than it is to have children cared for by a babysitter. According to the results of the study, infants benefit from being in the company of other babies on a daily basis.

Whereas some babies seem to show fear of strange adults, they are likely to reach out to try and touch an unfamiliar baby. The study even suggests that children as young as one year old can form friendships. Two of the children in the study were especially close. It was reported that if the children were separated for any reason, they would start to cry. The only way to satisfy them was to allow them to be together.

If the findings are true, it may lead to an increase in the use of family-oriented daycare centers where children can spend more time with each other and less time with adults.

Questions

9. Why couldn't the girl student answer the questions correctly?
10. What can be inferred about the girl student?
11. How are some universities trying to help students with the problem?
12. According to the study, when do babies feel the most comfortable?
13. What does Dr. Richard Perlman do?
14. How do babies react to unfamiliar babies?
15. What is the best way to care for babies?
zh:
篇章一

科罗拉多州立大学的一位大二女生刚上大学时，第一次在考试上出了问题。她说自己考前准备得很充分，有时考前几周就开始复习，可一进考场就发现自己答不对题。她会因为紧张和恐惧而脑子一片空白，想不出答案。她成绩很低，让老师们很惊讶。

事实上，这个学生经历的情况叫做「考试焦虑」。因为学生为考试担忧、不安，脑子就不如平常好使。由于极度紧张和焦虑，学生无法清晰地书写或思考。

虽然低分常常是不良学习习惯的结果，但有时考试焦虑才是低分的原因。近来，考试焦虑已被认定为一个真实的问题，而不只是懒学生的借口或虚假解释。

大学里有一些专门的辅导课程，试图帮助有同样问题的学生。在这些课程中，辅导员教学生如何管理考试焦虑，以此帮助他们。有些大学会让学生做测试来测量他们的焦虑程度。如果测试显示焦虑水平很高，学生就要上短期课程，帮他们应对紧张情绪。这些课程教学生如何放松身体，训练学生在极度紧张的场合下保持镇定。通过控制紧张情绪，他们就能让头脑轻松运转，学过的知识在考试中自然就能顺利输出。

篇章二

最近，加利福尼亚州洛杉矶的儿童发展中心开展了一项为期五年的研究，考察婴儿对不同类型的人有何反应。研究结果表明，婴儿在别的宝宝身边似乎比在陌生的成年人身边更自在。

这一结果印证了理查德·珀尔曼博士的观点。他写过很多关于育儿的书。珀尔曼博士支持这项研究的结论，并补充说，把孩子和别的孩子放在一起——比如放在日托中心——比请保姆照看孩子更合理。根据研究结果，婴儿每天和其他宝宝相处是有益的。

有些宝宝似乎对陌生成年人表现出恐惧，但他们很可能会伸手去试着摸一个不熟悉的宝宝。研究甚至表明，一岁大的孩子就能建立友谊。研究中有两个孩子格外亲密。据报道，如果这两个孩子因为任何原因被分开，他们就会开始哭，唯一能安抚他们的办法就是让他们待在一起。

如果这些发现成立，可能会促使更多以家庭为导向的日托中心出现——在那里，孩子彼此相处的时间更多，与成年人相处的时间更少。

title: Test 3 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

The American patent system, provided for in the Constitution, was designed to encourage the creation and use of new technology. An inventor would describe an invention both in writing and with drawings, and submit the description with a model to a government official. This was a big improvement from the past, when patents were submitted directly to the Secretary of State.

Now, if the invention was judged to be new and useful, the official would give the inventor a patent. The patent meant that for 14 years — later changed to 17 years — the inventor owned the new invention. Inventors could license their ideas to manufacturers or just use them themselves. The government would not issue any other patent for the same idea, and the inventor could sue anyone who used the patented idea without paying the owner of the patent for permission to use it. A useful patent meant that the inventor could make a lot of money.

In exchange for this governmental protection, the government published the patent specifications, which provide enough information so that other people could understand the invention — thus adding to the generally available technological knowledge. And at the end of the 14 years, anyone could use the invention for free.

The idea behind the patent system was twofold: it would increase the amount of technology by providing a way for people to make money out of new ideas, and it would make new technology widely available by publicizing ideas that might otherwise be kept as trade secrets.

Passage Two

Robert Frost was born in San Francisco in 1875 and was sent at the age of 10 to live in New England, an area which inspired almost all of his poetry. He was educated at Dartmouth College, New England, and Harvard University. He became a schoolmaster for a short time and then a farm laborer. During this period he wrote poetry, but with little recognition.

From 1912 to 1915 he lived in New England, where he became friendly with several poets, including Edward Thomas, and published A Boy's Will in 1913 and North of Boston in 1914. In America, his poetry was soon admired, and he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize on four occasions between 1924 and 1943. He went on writing throughout his life, publishing Steeple Bush at the age of 72. He died in 1963.

Frost's poems are revolutionary because they lack the exaggeration of rhetoric. Many of his lines and sentences are plain, and in themselves nothing, but they are bound together and made beautiful by a calm eagerness of emotion. With his close, observant eye and touch, we can feel the daily activities of farming and the landscape that is their background. Mowing, apple picking, or mending a wall — these poems reflect a humane, quiet concern and satisfaction in their rhythms and their gentle lyricism. Often there is an explicit or near-explicit moral, though sometimes this is hinted at rather than stated, and frequently there is an almost proverbial tone.

We learned to trust Robert Frost. The very lack of glamour or display in his poems gives them stability and honesty.

Questions

9. What is the speaker mainly talking about?
10. What could the inventor do if the idea was used by someone without paying money?
11. What could the owner of the patent do to protect his patent after 14 years?
12. How did the patent system increase the amount of technology?
13. What do we learn about Robert Frost from the passage?
14. What does the speaker say about Frost's poems?
15. What is described in Frost's poetry, according to the passage?
zh:
篇章一

美国宪法规定的专利制度，旨在鼓励新技术的创造和使用。发明人要用文字并配以图纸描述一项发明，然后把说明书连同模型一起提交给一位政府官员。比起过去把专利直接呈交国务卿，这是很大的进步。

如果这项发明被判定为新颖且有用，官员就会授予发明人专利。专利意味着在 14 年内（后来改为 17 年）这项新发明归发明人所有。发明人可以把想法授权给制造商，也可以自己使用。政府不会再就同一想法颁发其他专利，发明人可以起诉任何使用该专利想法、却没有向专利权人付费取得许可的人。一项有用的专利意味着发明人能赚很多钱。

作为这种政府保护的交换，政府会公布专利说明书，其中提供足够的信息，让别人也能理解这项发明——从而充实了可普遍获得的技术知识。而 14 年期满后，任何人都可以免费使用这项发明。

专利制度背后的想法有两层：一是为人们提供靠新想法赚钱的途径，从而增加技术的总量；二是通过公开那些原本可能被当作商业秘密保留下来的想法，让新技术广为可用。

篇章二

罗伯特·弗罗斯特 1875 年出生于旧金山，10 岁时被送到新英格兰生活，那片地方几乎激发了他所有的诗作。他先后就读于新英格兰的达特茅斯学院和哈佛大学。他当过很短时间的教师，之后又做过农场雇工。这期间他写诗，但没什么人认可。

1912 至 1915 年他住在新英格兰，与包括爱德华·托马斯在内的几位诗人交好，并于 1913 年出版《一个男孩的心愿》、1914 年出版《波士顿以北》。在美国，他的诗很快受到赞赏，1924 至 1943 年间四次获得普利策奖。他一生笔耕不辍，72 岁时还出版了《尖塔丛》。他于 1963 年去世。

弗罗斯特的诗是革命性的，因为它们没有修辞的夸张。他的许多诗句都很朴素，本身似乎什么也不是，却由一种平静而热切的情感串联起来，变得优美。凭借他细致敏锐的眼光和笔触，我们能感受到农事劳作与作为背景的风景。割草、摘苹果、修补围墙——这些诗以它们的节奏和温和的抒情，传达出一种富有人情味的、安静的关切与满足。诗中常常有明确或近乎明确的寓意，有时只是暗示而非明说，而且往往带有一种近乎谚语的语调。

我们学会了信任罗伯特·弗罗斯特。他的诗正因为毫无浮华与炫耀，才显得沉稳而诚实。

题目

9. 讲话者主要在谈什么？
10. 如果别人没付钱就使用了这个想法，发明人可以怎么做？
11. 14 年期满后，专利权人还能做什么来保护自己的专利？
12. 专利制度如何增加了技术的总量？
13. 从文中我们了解到罗伯特·弗罗斯特的什么？
14. 讲话者如何评价弗罗斯特的诗？
15. 根据文章，弗罗斯特的诗里描写了什么？

title: Test 4 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

The average person learns most of the 30,000 to 40,000 words whose meanings we recognize by hearing them or getting familiar with them in context without conscious effort. The best way to build a good vocabulary, therefore, is to read a great deal and to participate in a lot of good conversations. There are relatively few words that we learn permanently by purposefully referring to dictionaries or keeping word lists.

Here are some suggestions on how to do it.

Read plenty of good books. When you come across a new word or a new meaning of an old word, stop and see if you can understand it from its context. If you can't, and if you can manage without interrupting the thought of the book too much, look it up in the dictionary or ask somebody, and then repeat its meaning to yourself a couple of times. If you are really conscientious, write the word and its meaning in a personal vocabulary list. Go over the list from time to time. Further, try to use the new word in writing or conversation a few times over the next several days.

Listen to good conversations and be alert to new words you hear or to new meanings of words you have already known. Then treat them just as you treat the new words you read.

Learn and be alert to the parts of words: prefixes, suffixes and roots. Knowing them enables you to make intelligent guesses about the meanings of words.

Passage Two

Telephone books in the United States have white, blue and yellow pages. The white pages list people with phones by last name. The blue pages contain numbers of city services, government agencies and public schools. Businesses and professional services are listed in a special section, the yellow pages.

To make a long distance call, you need an area code. Each area in the US has an area code. The area covered by one area code may be small or large. For example, New York City has one area code, but so does the whole state of Oregon. If you want to know the area code of a place, you can look it up in the area map, which is printed in the front of the white pages.

There are a lot of public telephones in the US; they have their own numbers. If you are making a long distance call on a public phone and run out of money, give the number on your phone to the person you're talking to, then hang up the receiver and he can call you back. If you make a long distance call and get a wrong number, call the operator and explain what happened. This means that you can make the call again to the right number without having to pay more money.

Questions

9. According to the speaker, which is the best way to build your vocabulary?
10. When you meet a new word in reading, what are you suggested to do first?
11. What should you do with new words when you participate in a conversation?
12. In a telephone book, where can you find the number of a city council?
13. What should you check in a telephone book for a long distance call?
14. How can you avoid losing contact when making calls on public phones without much money left?
15. What should you do if you get a wrong number in making a long distance call?
zh:
篇章一

普通人认识的三万到四万个词，其词义大多是在听人说话或在语境中渐渐熟悉而习得的，并没有刻意努力。因此，积累良好词汇量的最佳方式就是大量阅读、多参与高质量的交谈。靠有意识地查词典或背单词表而长期记住的词，其实相当少。

以下是一些做法建议。

大量阅读好书。遇到一个新词，或者一个旧词的新含义时，停下来看看能否从上下文猜出它的意思。如果猜不出来，而又不至于太打断对书中内容的思考，就查词典或问问别人，然后把词义对自己重复几遍。如果你真的很认真，就把这个词和它的意思写进个人的词汇表，时不时翻一翻。此外，在接下来的几天里，试着在写作或交谈中用上这个新词几次。

多听高质量的交谈，留神你听到的新词，或你已经认识的词的新含义。然后像对待阅读中遇到的新词那样对待它们。

学习和留意词的构成部分：前缀、后缀和词根。掌握它们，你就能对词义做出有根据的猜测。

篇章二

美国的电话簿分白页、蓝页和黄页。白页按姓氏列出装了电话的人。蓝页登载市政服务、政府机构和公立学校的号码。企业和专业服务则列在一个专门的部分——黄页里。

打长途电话需要一个区号。美国每个地区都有区号。一个区号覆盖的区域可大可小。例如，纽约市只有一个区号，而整个俄勒冈州也只有一个区号。如果你想知道某个地方的区号，可以查印在白页前面的区号地图。

美国有很多公用电话，它们都有自己的号码。如果你在公用电话上打长途时钱用完了，就把你这台电话上的号码告诉对方，然后挂断，对方可以给你打回来。如果你打长途打错了号码，就给接线员打电话说明情况。这意味着你可以重新拨正确的号码，而不用多付钱。

题目

title: Test 5 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

We know that we have to pay for what we get. If we buy food, we know there will be a bill to pay. These are private bills. But there are also public bills that must be paid. Public bills are paid for by the government. In turn, we get these services through taxes.

What would happen if everyone in the city stopped paying taxes? The water supply would stop. Water might even become unclean and impure. The streets might not be cleaned. There would be no police force to protect people and property. Schools would be closed. People would become sick and diseases might spread. We should not want to live in such a city.

We all want pure water and food, clean streets and good schools. We want police to prevent us from crime. The chief duty of every government is to protect persons and property. More than three quarters of the money spent by our government is used for this purpose. The next large amount of public money goes to teach and train our citizens. Billions of dollars each year are spent on schools and libraries. Public money is used to pay the teachers and all the public officials. Also, a large amount of public funds is spent on roads.

The greatest part of the needed funds is raised by taxes. A tax is money that we all must pay to support the government. The law orders us to pay taxes; we have no choice in the matter. Almost everyone pays some taxes in one form or another.

Passage Two

As a result of rising university costs, many students are finding it necessary to take on part-time jobs. To make finding those jobs easier, the placement service has put together a listing of what is available locally. For some students, these part-time jobs could lead to full-time work after graduation, as they may offer experience in their own field — like finance, marketing or even management.

For example, National Savings Bank offers work on a half-time basis — that's 20 hours a week. Retail stores and restaurants have positions requiring fewer hours. Even less time is expected of those providing childcare. We have a number of families registered with us who are looking for babysitters for as few as four hours a week.

For students who prefer outdoor work, there are seasonal positions right on campus, working with the gardening and landscaping teams. These often require the most time, and they are the least flexible in terms of scheduling. To see a complete list of these and other available jobs — including the salary offered and the hours required — stop by our office and be sure to bring a resume with you. When you find something that interests you, we'll put you in touch with the person offering it. In addition, our counselors will give you hints about successful interviewing.

Questions

9. According to the speaker, what will happen if the citizens stop paying taxes?
10. In what way is the next large amount of public money used?
11. What message does the speaker want to convey in this talk?
12. What do we know about the placement service from the passage?
13. Which job requires the most time, according to the passage?
14. What should students bring with them to the office?
15. What will the counselors at the office help students do?
zh:
篇章一

我们知道，得到什么就得为之付钱。买食品，我们知道要付账单——这些是私人账单。但也有必须支付的公共账单，公共账单由政府支付；反过来，我们通过纳税获得这些服务。

如果城里所有人都不再纳税，会发生什么？供水中断，水甚至可能变得不洁、不纯净；街道可能没人清扫；没有警察保护人身和财产；学校关门；人们生病，疾病可能蔓延。我们不会想住在这样的城市里。

我们都想要干净的水和食物、清洁的街道和好学校；我们希望警察保护我们免受犯罪侵害。每个政府的首要职责就是保护人身和财产，我国政府开支中四分之三以上用于这一目的。下一笔大额公共开支用于教育和培训公民，每年有数十亿美元花在学校和图书馆上。公共资金用来支付教师和所有公职人员的薪水，还有大量公共资金花在道路上。

所需资金的最大部分靠税收筹集。税是我们所有人都必须缴纳、用来支持政府的钱。法律要求我们纳税，这件事上我们没有选择。几乎每个人都以某种形式缴纳一些税。

篇章二

由于大学费用上涨，许多学生发现不得不做兼职。为了让学生更容易找到这类工作，就业服务中心整理了一份本地可应聘岗位的清单。对一些学生来说，这些兼职可能通向毕业后的全职工作，因为它们能提供本专业领域的经验——比如金融、市场营销甚至管理。

例如，国民储蓄银行提供半职工作，即每周 20 小时。零售店和餐厅的岗位所需时间更少。提供儿童看护的岗位所需时间还更少——我们这儿登记了不少家庭，他们招保姆，每周只要四小时。

对于喜欢户外工作的学生，校园里就有季节性的岗位，跟园艺和景观团队一起干活。这类岗位往往耗时最多，在排班上也是最不灵活的。要看这些及其他岗位的完整清单——包括提供的薪水和工作时数——请到我们办公室来，务必带上简历。当你找到感兴趣的工作时，我们会帮你联系提供岗位的人。此外，我们的辅导员还会给你一些面试成功的提示。

题目

title: Test 6 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

The number of speakers of English in Shakespeare's time is estimated to have been about 5 million. Today it is estimated that some 300 million people speak it as a native language, mainly in the United States, Canada, Great Britain, Ireland, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. In addition to the standard varieties of English found in these areas, there are a great many regional and social varieties of the language, as well as various levels of usage that are employed both in its spoken and written forms.

In fact, it is impossible to estimate the number of people in the world who have acquired an adequate working knowledge of English in addition to their own language. The purposes for English learning, and the situations in which such learning takes place, are so varied that it is difficult to explain — and still more difficult to judge — what forms an adequate working knowledge for each situation.

The main reason for the widespread demand for English is its present importance as a world language. Besides serving the indefinite needs of its native speakers, English is a language in which some of the important works in science, technology and other fields are being produced — and not always by native speakers. It is widely used for such purposes as airport communications, international conferences, and the spread of information over the radio and television networks of many nations. It is a language of wider communication for a number of developing countries, especially former British colonies. Many of these countries have multilingual populations and need a language for internal communication in such matters as government, commerce, industry, law and education, as well as for international communication and for entrance to the scientific and technological developments in the West.

Passage Two

The podcast revolution is erupting all over the world, and seemingly all at once. Why is it getting so popular? The technology is simple to master and podcasting software is inexpensive — sometimes even free.

Two Chinese students are receiving international fame as millions of people around the world watch them podcast from their dormitory. They are called the "Back Dormitory Boys," and they specialize in miming Backstreet Boys songs. Although most people in China don't have iPods, podcasting is sweeping the country. The Back Dormitory Boys are among the thousands of Chinese who are putting their own homemade audio and video up on the internet for all to enjoy.

"You just gotta love two guys making a fool of themselves and gaining international attention," says Good Morning America technology expert Becky Worley.

The internet is becoming more and more popular with China's youth. About 60 percent of the 100 million Chinese who use the internet are under the age of 24. "This generation grew up with values that are very, very similar to their peers in the United States," said Huang Hong, publisher of Time in Beijing. "You're going to see a complete change in the cultural landscape of China."

Already, podcasting has taken off in the United States. Earlier this year, 19-year-old Gary Brolsma skyrocketed to internet fame with what he calls his "Numa Numa dance" — a lip sync to a Romanian pop song.

Questions

9. What is this speaker mainly talking about?
10. According to the passage, what is hard to estimate about English?
11. What is one of the situations when English is widely used?
12. Why do some former British colonies widely use English?
13. Why is podcasting sweeping the world?
14. What does podcasting mean, according to the speaker?
15. Why does the speaker hold that the internet is very popular among young people in China?
zh:
篇章一

莎士比亚时代说英语的人数据估计约为五百万。今天，估计约有三亿人把英语作为母语使用，主要在美国、加拿大、英国、爱尔兰、南非、澳大利亚和新西兰。除了这些地区的标准英语变体之外，英语还有大量地域性和社会性变体，以及在口语和书面语中使用的各种语域层次。

事实上，世界上有多少人在母语之外掌握了足以应付工作的英语，是无法估算的。学英语的目的和学英语的情境千差万别，因此很难说清——更难判断——在每种情境下什么才算「足以应付工作的知识」。

英语被广泛需求的主要原因，是它当前作为世界语言的重要性。除了满足母语者不确定的需要之外，英语还是产出科学、技术等领域一些重要著作所使用的语言——而且并不总是由母语者写出。它被广泛用于机场通讯、国际会议，以及通过许多国家的广播电视网传播信息。对不少发展中国家、尤其是前英国殖民地来说，英语是更广范围内交流的语言。这些国家中很多人口多语，需要一种语言用于政府、商业、工业、法律和教育等内部交流，也用于国际交流，以及接触西方的科技发展。

篇章二

播客革命正在全世界爆发，而且似乎是同时爆发。它为什么这么受欢迎？因为这项技术容易掌握，播客软件也不贵——有时甚至免费。

两名中国学生正在国际上走红，全世界数百万人在网上看他们在宿舍里录的播客。他们被称为「后舍男生」，专长是对口型模仿后街男孩的歌。虽然中国大多数人没有 iPod，播客却正在风靡全国。后舍男生是成千上万把自己的音视频作品上传到网上供人观赏的中国人之一。

《早安美国》的科技专家贝基·沃利说：「你没法不喜欢这两个出丑卖乖、却赢得国际关注的家伙。」

互联网在中国年轻人中越来越受欢迎。中国一亿网民中约 60% 不到 24 岁。《时代》周刊北京分社出版人黄鸿说：「这一代人成长时所持的价值观，与他们的美国同龄人非常非常相似。你们将会看到中国文化面貌的彻底改变。」

在美国，播客早已兴起。今年早些时候，19 岁的加里·布罗尔斯马凭他所谓的「Numa Numa 舞」——对一首罗马尼亚流行歌曲对口型——迅速在网上走红。

题目

9. 讲话者主要在谈什么？
10. 根据文章，关于英语有什么难以估算？
11. 英语被广泛使用的场合之一是哪里？
12. 一些前英国殖民地为什么广泛使用英语？
13. 播客为什么风靡世界？
14. 按讲话者的说法，播客是什么意思？
15. 讲话者为什么认为互联网在中国年轻人中很受欢迎？

title: Test 7 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

A new enemy is threatening Japanese traditions: leisure. As part of its attempt to increase imports, the government is trying to get people to work less and spend more. The workers are disgusted.

The figures support the Western prejudice that the Japanese are all work and no play. Trying to force workers away from their desks and machines, the government said last April that the country should cut down from its 2,100-hour average work year to 1,899 hours and a five-day week, beginning in February. Banks and stock markets will be closed on Saturdays. Staff of the civil service will be forced out of their offices two Saturdays a month. The government hopes that others will follow that practice. But some persuasion will be needed. Small companies are very angry about it and they fear competitors may not cut hours.

The unions are no happier. They have even advertised in newspapers arguing their case against the foreign pressure that is forcing leisure upon them. They say that shorter hours are a disguised pay cut. The industrialists, who have no objection to the government's plans, admit that shorter hours will help them cut costs.

Younger Japanese, who are supposed to be acting against their hard-working parents, show no sign of wanting time off either. But unlike older workers, they do spend money in their spare time. Not content with watching television, they dance, dress up, sit in cafes, go to pop concerts and generally drive the leisure-industry boom. Now that they know how to consume, maybe the West can teach them to relax and enjoy themselves, too.

Passage Two

Over the past decade, the environmental movement has exploded onto the minds of mainstream consumers — a fact not lost on marketers and advertisers. Green advertising started in the mid-1980s, when issues of the environment muscled their way to the forefront of marketing. Advertisers saw the consumer desire for environmentally safe products and tried to meet the demand as quickly as possible.

Not surprisingly, this first wave suffered from rough and poorly conceived marketing efforts. Many advertisers embraced a genuine concern for the environment, but consumers realized that some companies made false claims and exploited the movement, using such nebulous terms as "environmentally friendly" and "green." Consumers grew wary of environmental appeals, and advertisers reacted by reducing its emphasis.

Two legal guidelines paved the road to a second wave. In 1992, the Federal Trade Commission established guidelines for green marketing, followed shortly by state governments. California passed particularly stringent laws, setting definitions for terms like "ozone friendly," "biodegradable" and "recycled." According to the state's court, California seeks to guard against potentially specious claims or ecological puffery about products with minimal environmental attributes. Texas, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Tennessee, Connecticut and Washington soon followed the Golden State's lead.

The rigid regulations have left a number of advertisers confused and frustrated. Although some feel that environmental claims have already peaked and are on their way out, some believe that we've now entered green advertising's third wave, where environmental concerns are now part of the mainstream.

Questions

9. What is the purpose of getting the Japanese to have more spare time?
10. What does the union think of the shorter-hour system?
11. Which group of people welcomes the shorter-hour system in Japan?
12. What do we learn about the younger Japanese according to the passage?
13. What were some early problems with the first wave of green advertisements?
14. What do we know about consumers from the passage?
15. How did green advertisements change after the first wave?
zh:
篇章一

一个新的敌人正在威胁日本的传统：休闲。作为增加进口的一项举措，政府正设法让民众少工作、多消费，而工人们对此十分反感。

数据支持了西方人「日本人只知工作、不会玩乐」的偏见。为了把工人从办公桌和机器旁赶走，政府去年四月宣布，全国平均年工时应从 2100 小时降到 1899 小时，并从二月起实行五天工作周。银行和股市周六休市；公务员每月有两个周六被「请出」办公室。政府希望其他行业也照此办理，但这还需要一些说服工作。小公司对此非常愤怒，它们担心竞争对手不会减少工时。

工会更不高兴。他们甚至在报纸上登广告，为自己的立场辩护，反对那种强迫他们休闲的外国压力。他们说，缩短工时不过是变相的降薪。而资方对政府的计划并无异议，他们承认缩短工时有助于降低成本。

年轻一代的日本人本该反抗他们勤劳的父母，可他们也毫无想要休息的迹象。但与年长的劳动者不同，他们确实会在业余时间花钱。他们不满足于看电视，还去跳舞、打扮、泡咖啡馆、听流行音乐会，总体上推动着休闲产业的繁荣。既然他们已懂得如何消费，也许西方可以教他们如何放松和享受生活。

篇章二

过去十年间，环保运动冲进了主流消费者的意识——营销者和广告人对此心知肚明。绿色广告始于 20 世纪 80 年代中期，当时环境议题挤进了营销的最前沿。广告人看到了消费者对环保安全产品的渴望，便尽可能迅速地去满足这一需求。

毫不奇怪，这第一波浪潮受累于粗糙、思虑不周的营销手法。许多广告人确实真心关注环境，但消费者发现，有些公司做出虚假宣称、利用这场运动，使用「环保友好」「绿色」这类含糊的词语。消费者对环保诉求变得警惕，广告人便相应降低了强调的程度。

两条法律指引为第二波浪潮铺了路。1992 年，联邦贸易委员会制定了绿色营销准则，各州政府很快跟进。加利福尼亚通过了尤其严格的法律，为「不破坏臭氧层」「可生物降解」「再生」等词确定了定义。据该州法院的说法，加州旨在防范对环保属性极小的产品作出可能虚假的宣称或生态吹嘘。得克萨斯、马萨诸塞、明尼苏达、田纳西、康涅狄格和华盛顿等州很快效仿了这个「金州」。

严格的规定让不少广告人困惑、沮丧。尽管有人认为环保宣称的高峰已过、正在退场，也有人相信我们已进入绿色广告的第三波浪潮——环境关切如今已成为主流的一部分。

题目

9. 让日本人拥有更多闲暇时间的目的是什么？
10. 工会如何看待缩短工时制度？
11. 在日本，哪一群人欢迎缩短工时制度？
12. 根据文章，关于年轻一代日本人我们了解到什么？
13. 第一波绿色广告有哪些早期问题？
14. 从文中我们了解到消费者的什么？
15. 第一波之后，绿色广告发生了怎样的变化？

title: Test 8 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

In America, driver's education is part of the regular high school curriculum. Every student in his or her second year of high school is required to take a class in driver's education. However, unlike other courses, it is not given during the regular school year; instead it is a summer course. The course is divided into two parts: class time for learning laws and regulations, and driving time to practice.

Driving class time is not unlike any other class. The students have a text from which they study the basic laws they must know. Driving time is a chance for the students to practice starting, steering, backing up, parking, switching lanes, turning corners and all the other maneuvers required.

Each student is required to drive a total of six hours. The students are divided into groups of four. The students and the instructor go out driving for two hours. Thus each student gets half an hour driving time per outing. The instructor and the driver sit in the front seats, and the other three students sit in the back.

Driver's education cars are unlike other cars in that they have two sets of brakes — one on the driver's side and one on the other side where the instructor sits. Thus, if the student driver should run into difficulties, the instructor can take over. The car also has another special feature: on the top of the car is a sign that reads "Student Driver," which lets nearby drivers know that they should use extra caution, because the student driver is not very experienced and is prone to driving slowly.

Passage Two

The pioneer of chocolate cookies in America is Amos Cookies. Amos was a talent agent at the William Morris Agency who used home-baked chocolate chip cookies as a calling card. After a while, some of his famous clients began encouraging him to sell the cookies. They even invested in the Famous Amos Cookie Company, which he started in 1975, making him one of the pioneers of the gourmet cookie trend. Sales at Famous Amos hit 12 million dollars by 1982.

His cookies were a success, but he was no manager, and his company started losing money. Amos had to bring in new money. From 1985 to 1988, he went through four different co-owners. Each time a change was made, Amos gave up more of his share of the pie. By the time the Shanby Group bought it in 1988, Amos had nothing left. He even signed away his trademark "Amos."

In 1992, when he started a new company called Wally Amos Presents Chip and Cookie, the Famous Amos Corporation sued him for infringement and libel. After an acrimonious dispute, Wally Amos agreed not to use his own name or a caricature of himself on the cookies, and not to bad-mouth the company that owned his name. Wally Amos then moved to Hawaii and started another cookie company called the Uncle No-Name Cookie Company.

This case is an excellent demonstration of the dangers of trademark ownership for entrepreneurs.

Questions

9. What is special about the driver's course in America?
10. What can students learn during class time?
11. How many times should a student go out driving in total?
12. How is the driver's education car designed in order to prevent accidents?
13. What kind of company was Amos with in the beginning?
14. Why did Amos begin to lose money after his initial success?
15. Why couldn't Amos even use his name on his cookies after 1988?
zh:
篇章一

在美国，驾驶教育是高中常规课程的一部分。每个高二学生都必须修一门驾驶教育课。但与其它课程不同，它不在正常学年中开设，而是暑期课程。这门课分两部分：学习法规的课堂时间，以及练习驾驶的上路时间。

驾驶课的课堂跟其他课没什么不同。学生有一本教材，用来学习他们必须掌握的基本法规。上路时间则让学生练习起步、转向、倒车、停车、变道、转弯以及所有其他要求的操作。

每个学生总共必须驾驶六小时。学生被分成四人一组，学生和教练一起出去开两小时，因此每人每次上车有半小时的驾驶时间。教练和驾驶的学生坐前排，另外三名学生坐后排。

教练车与其他车不同，它有两套刹车——一套在驾驶座一侧，一套在教练所坐的另一侧。这样，如果学生驾驶时遇到困难，教练可以接管。这车还有另一个特点：车顶有一块牌子，写着「学员驾驶」，让附近的司机知道要格外小心，因为学员经验不足，往往开得很慢。

篇章二

美国巧克力饼干的先驱是阿莫斯饼干。阿莫斯原本是威廉·莫里斯经纪公司的一名星探，他把自家烤的巧克力碎饼干当作名片送人。过了一段时间，他的一些明星客户开始鼓励他卖饼干，甚至投资了他 1975 年创办的「著名的阿莫斯饼干公司」，这使他成为精品饼干潮流先驱之一。到 1982 年，「著名的阿莫斯」的销售额达到 1200 万美元。

他的饼干很成功，但他不是个管理者，公司开始亏损。阿莫斯不得不引入新的资金。1985 到 1988 年间，他先后经历了四任不同的合伙人。每一次变动，阿莫斯都让出更多自己那一份。等到 1988 年尚比集团收购时，阿莫斯已一无所有——他甚至签字让出了「阿莫斯」这个商标。

1992 年，他创办了一家新公司「沃利·阿莫斯呈现饼干与曲奇」，「著名的阿莫斯公司」便以侵权和诽谤起诉他。经过一场激烈的争执，沃利·阿莫斯同意不在饼干上使用自己的姓名或自己的漫画像，也不再说他名字所属公司的坏话。之后沃利·阿莫斯搬到夏威夷，又开了一家饼干公司，叫「无名大叔饼干公司」。

这个案例极好地说明了商标所有权对创业者意味着何种风险。

题目

9. 美国的驾驶课有什么特别之处？
10. 学生在课堂上能学到什么？
11. 一个学生总共要出去驾驶多少次？
12. 教练车为防止事故做了怎样的设计？
13. 阿莫斯起初在哪类公司工作？
14. 阿莫斯在初步成功之后为什么会开始亏损？
15. 1988 年之后，阿莫斯为什么连自己的名字都不能用在饼干上？

title: Test 9 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

There is no doubt that adults, and even highly educated adults, vary greatly in the speed and efficiency of their reading. Some proceed very slowly throughout; others dash along too quickly and then have to go back again.

Poor readers in particular may lack the ability to vary their manner of reading according to the type of reading matter and their intentions in reading it. A good reader can move at great speed through the text of a novel or similar light reading matter. In reading more difficult material with the intention of taking in the whole of it, he will proceed more slowly; but even then he will vary his pace, concentrating on the key words and passages, rereading them several times, or passing more quickly over the remainder.

A less efficient reader tends to maintain the same speed whatever the material he reads. Therefore, even light reading matter gives him little pleasure, because he reads so slowly. But this pace may be too fast for really difficult material, which requires special concentration at difficult points.

A type of reading which needs careful attention to detail is proofreading. In order to detect misprints in a sample print, the reader needn't notice so much the meaning of what he reads as the exact shape and order of words in the text. This is extremely difficult for most people, since they are used to ignoring such details. In fact, considerable practice is required to perform this task efficiently, and it can be done only by reading very slowly and by paying comparatively little attention to the general meaning of the text.

Passage Two

Twenty-five years ago, Ray Anderson, a single parent with a one-year-old son, was returning home on Christmas Eve when he witnessed a horrible accident. The driver of a truck ran a red light and hit the car of Sandra Jenkins. That killed Sandra instantly, but her three-month-old daughter was trapped upside down in the burning wreckage.

While others looked on in horror, Anderson jumped out of his vehicle and crawled into the car through the shattered rear window to try to free the infant. Seconds later, the car was totally engulfed in flames, but Anderson was miraculously able to pull the baby to safety. While the child came out of the accident virtually uninjured, Anderson was bleeding massively over half of his body. Two hours later, Anderson died — but this heroic act was published widely in the media.

Anderson's son was soon adopted by relatives, and the family moved to the East Coast.

What really drew public attention were some other details beyond the accident. According to the newspaper, Anderson was on a mission of love that fateful Christmas Eve, in the process of distributing care packages to needy families in the area. That was a yearly tradition that he performed unbeknownst to everyone. This he did because of his firm conviction that the best Christmas gifts came not from the gifts received but from those given, and that those acts of charity should remain anonymous.

As it turns out, Sandra Jenkins was also involved in similar volunteer work throughout the community.

"Merry Christmas. Share this remarkable Christmas story with all of you — courage, life and love."

Questions

9. What idea does the speaker mainly want to convey?
10. How do good readers read a novel?
11. What is typical of inefficient readers in terms of reading speed?
12. What does proofreading require?
13. What event did Ray Anderson witness at the beginning of the story?
14. How did Ray save the baby?
15. What was Ray doing on that fateful Christmas Eve?
zh:
篇章一

毫无疑问，成年人、甚至受过高等教育的成年人，在阅读速度和效率上差别很大。有些人通篇读得很慢，另一些人则冲得太快，然后不得不回头再读。

尤其是阅读能力差的人，可能缺乏根据阅读材料类型和阅读目的调整阅读方式的能力。好的读者能以很快的速度读完一部小说或类似的轻松读物。而在阅读较难的材料、并打算通篇理解时，他会读得慢一些；但即便那时，他也会变换速度：把注意力集中在关键词和关键段落上，反复重读几遍，其余部分则较快带过。

效率较低的读者往往不论读什么材料都保持同一速度。因此，即便是轻松的读物也让他得不到什么乐趣，因为他读得太慢。而这个速度对真正困难的材料又可能太快，因为难处需要格外集中注意力。

需要仔细注意细节的一类阅读是校对。要在样张中找出印刷错误，读者不必太注意所读内容的意思，而要留意文中单词的确切形状和顺序。这对大多数人来说极其困难，因为他们习惯于忽略这类细节。事实上，要高效完成这项任务需要大量练习，而且只能通过非常缓慢地阅读、并相对少地关注全文大意才能做到。

篇章二

25 年前，带着一岁儿子的单亲父亲雷·安德森在平安夜回家途中，目睹了一场可怕的车祸。一辆卡车的司机闯红灯，撞上了桑德拉·詹金斯的车。桑德拉当场死亡，但她三个月大的女儿头朝下被困在燃烧的残骸里。

当旁人惊恐地看着时，安德森跳下车，从破碎的后车窗爬进车里，试图救出婴儿。几秒钟后，汽车完全被火焰吞没，但安德森奇迹般地把孩子拉到了安全处。孩子在这场事故中几乎没有受伤，而安德森半身以上大量出血。两小时后，安德森去世了——但他的英勇事迹被媒体广泛报道。

安德森的儿子很快被亲戚收养，一家人搬到了东海岸。

真正引起公众关注的，是事故之外的一些细节。据报纸报道，在那个决定命运的平安夜，安德森正执行一项爱的使命——给这一带的贫困家庭送去关怀礼包。那是他每年都做、却不为人知的传统。他这样做，是因为他坚信最好的圣诞礼物不是收到的礼物，而是送出的礼物，而且这些善举应当不留姓名。

事实证明，桑德拉·詹金斯也一直在社区里做着类似的志愿服务。

「圣诞快乐。把这个非凡的圣诞故事分享给你们所有人——勇气、生命与爱。」

题目

9. 讲话者主要想传达什么观点？
10. 好的读者怎样读小说？
11. 就阅读速度而言，低效读者的典型特点是什么？
12. 校对需要什么？
13. 故事开头雷·安德森目睹了什么事件？
14. 雷是怎样救出婴儿的？
15. 在那个决定命运的平安夜，雷正在做什么？

title: Test 10 · 听力篇章
en:
Passage One

A beetle invasion in the United States has killed at least 20 million ash trees. The invasion of the emerald ash borer was first discovered near Detroit, Michigan. Experts believe the small green insects arrived in the 1990s in shipments of goods from East Asia. The emerald ash borer has destroyed trees in the Midwest and as far east in the United States as Maryland. The insects have also spread as far north as Ontario, Canada.

Ash trees can resist many diseases, but they cannot resist the emerald ash borer. It lays eggs on the bark. The young larvae drill into and feed on the inner bark. This harms the ability of the tree to transport water and nutrition.

In some places, farmers are using detection trees. They have an area where bark has been cut away. The area circles the tree. The process weakens the tree. It makes them easier targets for borers, and shows if the insects are nearby.

Efforts to stop the spread of the emerald ash borer include cutting down affected trees. There are worries that the ash tree might disappear unless the invasion is controlled. To prepare for such a possibility, a government laboratory is asking people to send in the seeds from ash trees. It examines and X-rays the seeds to make sure there are no living borer fertilized eggs; only the best seeds are retained and then sent for storage in a seed bank. There they are dried and frozen. Should the seeds ever be needed, the hope is that scientists might someday develop an ash tree that could resist the little green attackers.

Passage Two

Majestic. Serene. Just two words to describe the scenic regions of Utah in the mountain West of the United States. Now our office offers fabulous five-day outdoor packages to the state for the adventurous.

On the first day of your tour, visit the capital of historic Salt Lake City — Temple Square, home to the world-famous Mormon Tabernacle Choir, and other local historical sites. Then your tour will take you on a four-day adventure of a lifetime to central and southern Utah, where you will hike and backpack through Arches National Park, Goblin Valley and Bryce National Park. You'll also explore the magical world of Little Wild Horse Canyon. This very narrow, winding chasm, with its steep walls on either side of you, will leave you in amazement, knowing that it was formed from rushing water and erosion over millions of years.

You'll also hike and scramble up to remote Indian ruins, study their history along the way, and learn how to respect and preserve the sites and wildlife you encounter. You also learn the basics in rappelling techniques designed specifically for the amateur climber.

The price of your package includes local transportation in Utah, one night's lodging in a four-star hotel in Salt Lake City, hiking and camping gear, two meals a day, and your professional tour guide. Transportation from your point of origin is not included.

Contact our office between 8:00 and 5:30 PM for more information and current availability on this wilderness trek. And reservations must be made 13 days in advance. Let us show Utah like no one else can.

Questions

9. How did the emerald ash borers go to the United States, according to experts?
10. How far do the insects spread northward?
11. Why is part of the bark cut away?
12. What is the government laboratory trying to do?
13. What is the feature of the scenic regions of Utah?
14. Which activity is included in the package tour?
15. What is covered in the price of the tour?
zh:
篇章一

美国的一场甲虫入侵已导致至少两千万棵白蜡树死亡。这种「白蜡窄吉丁」的入侵最早在密歇根州底特律附近被发现。专家认为，这些绿色小虫是 20 世纪 90 年代随来自东亚的货物传入的。白蜡窄吉丁已毁掉美国中西部以及东部远至马里兰州的树木，还向北扩散到了加拿大的安大略省。

白蜡树能抵抗许多病害，却抵抗不了白蜡窄吉丁。它把卵产在树皮上，幼幼虫钻入并取食内层树皮，从而损害树木输送水分和养分的能力。

在一些地方，农民使用「诱测树」：在树上切掉一圈树皮，这一圈环绕树干。这样做会削弱树木，使它更容易成为吉丁的目标，同时也能显示附近是否有这种昆虫。

阻止白蜡窄吉丁扩散的措施包括砍伐受害树木。人们担心，如果不加控制，白蜡树可能会消失。为应对这种可能，一家政府实验室请人们寄来白蜡树的种子。实验室对种子进行检查和 X 光透视，确保没有活的吉丁受精卵；只有最好的种子被留下，送去种子库保存。在那里，种子被干燥、冷冻。万一将来需要这些种子，人们希望科学家有朝一日能培育出可以抵抗这种绿色小虫的白蜡树。

篇章二

雄伟。宁静。只用两个词就能形容美国西部山区犹他州的风景区。现在，我们办事处为爱冒险的人推出精彩的五日户外游套餐。

行程第一天，参观历史悠久的州府盐湖城——圣殿广场（世界著名的摩门教礼拜堂合唱团所在地）以及其他当地历史景点。随后，行程将带你在犹他州中部和南部度过毕生难忘的四天冒险：徒步并背包穿越拱门国家公园、地精谷和布莱斯国家公园。你还会探索「小野马峡谷」的神奇世界。这条非常狭窄、蜿蜒的峡谷两侧岩壁陡峭，会让你惊叹不已——要知道，它是数百万年间湍急的水流冲刷侵蚀而成的。

你还会徒步攀爬到偏远的印第安遗址，沿途了解它们的历史，并学习如何尊重和保护你遇到的遗址与野生动植物。你还会学到专为业余攀登者设计的基础速降技巧。

套餐价格包括犹他州当地交通、盐湖城四星级酒店一晚住宿、徒步与露营装备、每日两餐以及专业导游。出发地的交通不包括在内。

请在上午 8 点至下午 5 点 30 分之间联系我们的办事处，了解这次荒野徒步的更多信息和当前名额。预订须提前 13 天。让我们用独一无二的方式带你看犹他。

题目

9. 据专家说，白蜡窄吉丁是如何进入美国的？
10. 这种昆虫向北扩散到多远？
11. 为什么要切掉一部分树皮？
12. 这家政府实验室想做什么？
13. 犹他州风景区有何特点？
