8. 罗布·梅特卡夫出了什么事，他的时段可以由这位女士替代？
9. 情绪对人有什么影响？
10. 大多数人没有意识到的保持好心情的最佳方法是什么？
11. 按讲话者的说法，有氧运动为什么能让人振作？
12. 一些年轻人为什么说乡村生活已经死了？
13. 过去村民的生活是怎样的？
14. 按讲话者的看法，是什么带来了今天乡村生活的变化？
15. 讲话者如何看待今天的乡村生活？
16. 消除饥饿首先要做什么？
17. 联合国最近宣布的「饥饿项目」目标是什么？
18. 要维持我们所做的工作，什么至关重要？
19. 随着女性在经济上获得赋权，什么增加了？
20. 海伦·沃特曼的工作是什么？
21. 年轻人入学时常常问什么？
22. 海伦·沃特曼在学院训练中强调什么？
23. 从讲师的引言故事我们能学到什么？
24. 在大多数西方国家，问候常常包含什么？
25. 对美国人来说，什么被视为对食物满意的表示？

title: Model Test 6 · 综合训练
en:
Section A — Conversation One (Questions 1–4)

— I don't enjoy dating anymore. I can't seem to find anyone I have anything in common with.
— Don't feel discouraged. Be patient. As you are so distinguished, you will definitely find the person who is right for you.
— To tell you the truth, I'm tired of being alone. I hope to find my missus, right? What should I do?
— Do you believe in internet matchmaking service?
— That's really a new walk of life. What is it exactly?
— It helps match up singles the world over and helps find the man and woman of their dreams.
— Oh, it must be to the taste of a certain group of people.
— The advertisement said Dream Dates has matched up thousands of singles the world over.
— Unbelievable. They must be exaggerating the figure.
— Look at the way they manage their business. They collect applicants' photos and give the applicants questionnaires to fill out as to what type of character they are.
— I don't believe several questions can decide the type of person you are. People's characters are complicated and keep changing all the time.
— Anyway, it seems that things work well this way. The information and specifications will be entered in a large computer database.
— A computer to decide your best date? That's really ridiculous. Look, it promises Dream Dates provides expert dating service and a place for singles to meet. "Will introduce you to the person uniquely qualified to be your partner"? Sheer slogans, not reliable.
— It says you can enroll in a free trial membership.
— I won't do it even if they pay me for that.
— Well, we don't have to believe this. Maybe I can tell John and see whether he'd like to try it.

Section A — Conversation Two (Questions 5–8)

— With us now is Malcolm Bricklin, CEO of Visionary Vehicles. Hello.
— Hello, everyone.
— We have been hearing a couple of things about this — news that Ford Motor Company is slashing up to 30,000 jobs, shutting down 14 plants nationwide. Is it a big deal if we are no longer manufacturing these cars, Malcolm?
— I think it's a huge deal. I mean, the companies are massive employers, both directly and indirectly. If you look at Ford after their restructuring, they've actually got 87,000 employees, which is twice as many as Microsoft have worldwide. Moreover, if you look at those jobs, they are very high-paying jobs. These are people who can afford to buy their own products.
— Er, it seems to indicate a big hit for our economy if these jobs go bye-bye.
— Yeah, it's a really sad day for America.
— But it is not as if cars stop being made, right?
— Correct. Still a large number of cars are being made by American manufacturers. More than half of the American cars sold in America are American. So what has happened over time is that as the market share has fallen, foreign car companies have come in, taken over plants and set up new plants, and they have taken over that capacity. So it is not like there are fewer cars being produced in America than there were 30 years ago.
— Let me ask you about the Chinese coming in. What would it mean to American jobs if and when that happens?
— The Chinese cars we have seen so far aren't that great, and they don't have the branding necessary to make a huge impact on the world stage.

Section B — Passage One (Questions 9–11)

The economic costs of noise to society are several. Airports are currently operating at less capacity because of noise regulations which restrict their hours of operation. For instance, at Washington's National Airport, jet traffic is not allowed from 11 pm to 7 am. Other airports restrict the use of certain runways. One estimate is that noise restrictions reduce possible airport use by 20%. The profitable cargo trade is especially affected by night restrictions.

In the case of airports, jet engines may be modified to reduce their noise level. One estimate is that 5.7 billion dollars would be required to equip all existing jet engines with noise control devices. However, even taking this step will not reduce noise levels at all points to acceptable values. Some combination of methods is probably necessary.

If all aircraft were made quieter by existing methods, there would be a number of economic benefits. An increase in airport capacity would occur. Property values near airports might rise. Transportation costs to and from airports could be reduced, since the airports now could be located closer to population centers.

Much research still needs to be done on the economic aspects of noise reduction and noise effects. Although some of the effects of noise pollution are known, more must be discovered about its effects on health, productivity, property values and the quality of life. Furthermore, the cost of noise pollution to the economy as a whole needs to be investigated. The public must be alerted to the dangers and economic costs of noise pollution so that people may make intelligent choices and exert appropriate pressures.

Section B — Passage Two (Questions 12–15)

In the case of mobile phones, change is everything. Recent research indicates that the mobile phone is changing not only our culture but our very bodies as well.

First, let's talk about culture. The difference between the mobile phone and its parent, the fixed-line phone, is you get whoever answers it. This has several implications. The most common one, however, and perhaps the thing that has changed our culture forever, is the "meeting influence." People no longer need to make firm plans about when and where to meet. 20 years ago, a Friday night would need to be arranged in advance. Now, however, a night out can be arranged on the run.

Texting changes people as well. In their paper "Insights into the Social and Psychological Effects of SMS Text Messaging," two British researchers distinguished between two types of mobile phone users: the talkers and the texters — those who prefer voice to text message, and those who prefer text to voice. They found that the mobile phone's individuality and privacy gave texters the ability to express a whole new outer personality. Texters were likely to report that their family would be surprised if they were to read their texts.

Another scientist wrote of the changes that mobiles have brought to body language. There are two kinds that people use while speaking on the phone. There is the "speak-easy": the head is held high in a self-confident way, chatting away. And there is the "space-maker": these people focus on themselves and keep out other people.

Section C — Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

— Well, for years people have been trying to compete with their neighbors. How about actually trying to get along with them? Joining us with some simple tips on how to deal with those likable and not-so-likable neighbors is Betty Wong. She is the executive editor of Family Circle magazine. Good morning, Betty.
— Good morning, everyone.
— First, you might ask why it is important to have a good relationship with your neighbors. Well, you know, your home is your shelter, and how you get along with your neighbors really plays a large part in your health, well-being and happiness. And so it's important at least to establish a good, cordial, or at least polite relationship with your neighbors.
— When you move into a neighborhood, you should establish relationships. If the neighbors don't reach out to you, don't assume that they are being rude or unfriendly. After a few days, go ahead and introduce yourself, because I think once you make friends with them, it makes that much easier to prevent problems later on. Or maybe ask them for a favor, like if you are on vacation and you need them to water your plants and pick up your mail. It's much easier when you know them personally.
— Yeah, neighbors can be really, really helpful, but of course they can also be annoying. For example, loud music is one of those top complaints, and I think, you know, for most reasons, people probably aren't even aware that they are causing problems for their neighbors. And I think if you bring it up to your neighbor's attention, they will be more than happy to fix it. But don't just call the police. You could say something like, you know, "I'm really a light sleeper," or "I suffer from headaches. Can you help me out by turning down the music during those evening hours or the early morning?" Or come up with a compromise that works for both of you — a resolution that works for both of you.
— There is another really sensitive situation: unpleasant smells. But your neighbor is just as entitled to cook whatever she likes in the comfort of her own home. You should try to approach them politely, reasonably, and if that doesn't work, you could also just talk to management, because maybe there is something wrong with your building's ventilation system.
— Besides, this month's Family Circle mentions the power in numbers, which means sometimes it does help to get support from your fellow neighbors, but you have to be sensitive that you are not ganging up on your next-door neighbor. For more on this topic and others, you can refer to my magazine.

Section C — Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

The popularity of mobile devices has had some unintended and even dangerous consequences. We now know that mobile communications are linked to a significant increase in distracted driving, resulting in injury and loss of life.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reported that in this year, driver distraction was the cause of 18% of all fatal crashes, with 3,328 people killed, and crashes resulting in an injury, with 421,000 people wounded. 40% of all American teens say they have been in a car when the driver used a cell phone in a way that put people in danger, according to a survey. 11% of drivers aged 18 to 20 who were involved in an automobile accident and survived admitted they were sending or receiving texts when they crashed.

Distracted driving endangers life and property, and the current levels of injury and loss are unacceptable. To stop this problem, the FCC is working with industry safety organizations and other government agencies to inform and educate the public about the dangers of distracted driving, and is seeking to identify and facilitate the development of innovative technologies that could reduce the incidence of distracted driving. To help in this effort and share information, we created a dedicated website.

Currently, there is no national ban on texting or using a wireless phone while driving, but a number of states have passed laws banning texting or wireless phones or requiring hands-free use of wireless phones while driving.

Parents shall give teen drivers simple, clear instructions not to use their wireless devices while driving. According to the Cellular Telecommunications Industry Association, the easiest way to say it is: "On the road, off the phone." Before new drivers get their licenses, discuss the fact that taking their eyes off the road, even for a few seconds, could cost someone injury or even death.

Children learn from their parents' behavior. No one should text and drive. Be an example for your children, and if you need to text or talk on the phone, pull over to a safe place.

Become informed and be active. Review the information and the literature on our website. Set rules for yourself and your household regarding distracted driving. Tell family, friends, and organizations to which you belong about the importance of driving without distractions. Take information to your children's schools and ask that it be shared with students and parents.

Section C — Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

Sometime earlier this year, I took a trip to England and France to go see some friends in France. It was a wonderful trip; I really loved it. But one thing that struck me — I guess this would strike anyone whenever they travel — is how different cultures are from our own. Not just how different they are, but how similar. But I suppose it is the differences that really stand out.

One of the things that struck me very much was the difference in attitudes toward smoking. Many people know there's a growing anti-smoking sentiment in Europe. However, when I went to England and France, I got a new perspective on this issue. People seem to smoke anywhere and everywhere, even though anti-smoking signs are all over the public places.

I heard several times over the radio about a member of the World Cup soccer team who smoked. And people were actually saying, "Well, he shouldn't be on the team because he's a bad example for our children." I think if they want to look at bad examples for their children with smoking, they should just go out on the street, or go into the subways, or look in the mirror even, because so many of them are smoking in very inappropriate places.

I went to a restaurant in London and they had a buffet. There was this one Englishwoman who had her cigarette in her hand — lit cigarette. She was blowing smoke and holding her cigarette directly over the buffet food. Actually, when I talked to English people later, they were pretty shocked too, and they said that's even rude by even British standards.

It didn't just make me feel that the Europeans are bad. It also had, conversely, a positive effect on my attitudes toward American smokers. There are a lot of American smokers who will proclaim their right to smoke whenever they want, but they will follow the rules generally. In general, they do have consideration for other non-smokers, so this experience in Europe gave me more of a respect for this kind of smokers.

zh:
A 节 · 对话一（第 1—4 题）

—— 我不再喜欢约会了。我好像找不到一个跟我有共同点的人。
—— 别灰心，耐心点。你这么优秀，肯定能找到适合你的人。
—— 说实话，我厌倦单身了。我希望能找到我老婆——对吧？我该怎么办？
—— 你相信网络婚介服务吗？
—— 那真是种新活法。它到底是什么？
—— 它帮全世界的单身人士配对，帮他们找到梦想中的另一半。
—— 哦，那一定是合某些人的口味。
—— 广告说「梦幻约会」已经为全世界成千上万的单身人士配对成功。
—— 难以置信，他们一定夸大了数字。
—— 看看他们怎么做生意的。他们收集申请人的照片，还给申请人发问卷，问他们是什么性格类型。
—— 我不相信几个问题就能决定你是什么样的人。人的性格很复杂，而且一直在变。
—— 不管怎样，看起来这套办法运作得还不错。信息和各项条件会被录入一个大型计算机数据库。
—— 让计算机来选你最好的约会对象？那真是太荒唐了。你看，它承诺「梦幻约会」提供专业约会服务和一个单身者相识的场所，「将为你引见那位独一无二、有资格成为你伴侣的人」？纯是口号，不可靠。
—— 上面说你可以注册免费试用会员。
—— 就算他们给我钱我也不干。
—— 好吧，我们也不必信这个。也许我可以告诉约翰，看他想不想试试。

A 节 · 对话二（第 5—8 题）

—— 现在和我们连线的是「远见汽车」首席执行官马尔科姆·布里克林。你好。
—— 大家好。
—— 我们陆续听到一些消息：福特汽车公司要裁掉多达 3 万个岗位，关停全国 14 家工厂。马尔科姆，如果我们不再生产这些汽车，这是件大事吗？
—— 我认为这是件天大的事。我是说，这些公司无论直接还是间接都是巨大的雇主。看看福特重组之后，实际上还有 8.7 万名员工，是微软全球员工的两倍。而且，看看那些岗位，都是薪酬很高的岗位。这些人买得起自己生产的产品。
—— 呃，这似乎说明，如果这些岗位消失，我们的经济会受到重创。
—— 是啊，对美国来说这真是令人难过的一天。
—— 但并不是说汽车就不造了，对吧？
—— 对。美国制造商仍然在生产大量汽车。在美国销售的美国车中，一半以上是美国造的。所以这些年来发生的是：随着市场份额下降，外国汽车公司进来，接管了工厂、建了新厂，它们接手了那部分产能。所以美国生产的汽车并不比 30 年前少。
—— 我想问问中国车企进入的问题。如果真有那么一天，这对美国的就业意味着什么？
—— 我们目前看到的中国车并不怎么样，它们也缺少在世界舞台上产生巨大影响所需的品牌力。

B 节 · 篇章一（第 9—11 题）

噪声给社会带来的经济代价有好几项。由于限制运营时段的噪声法规，机场目前的运力低于满负荷。例如，华盛顿国家机场禁止喷气式飞机在晚上 11 点到早上 7 点之间起降。其他机场则限制某些跑道的使用。有估计认为，噪声限制使机场可用运力减少 20%。利润丰厚的货运尤其受夜间限制的影响。

就机场而言，可以改造喷气发动机以降低噪声水平。有估计认为，要给所有现役喷气发动机装备噪声控制装置，需要 57 亿美元。然而，即便采取这一措施，也无法把各处的噪声都降到可接受的水平。很可能需要多种方法结合使用。

如果用现有方法让所有飞机都更安静，会带来若干经济收益：机场容量会提高；机场附近的房产价值可能上升；往返机场的交通成本可以降低，因为机场现在可以建得离人口中心更近。

关于降噪和噪声影响的经济层面，还有大量研究要做。虽然噪声污染的某些影响已知，但它在健康、生产率、房产价值和生活质量方面的影响还需进一步弄清。此外，噪声污染对整个经济造成的代价也需要调查。必须让公众意识到噪声污染的危险和经济代价，这样人们才能做出明智的选择并施加适当的压力。

B 节 · 篇章二（第 12—15 题）

就手机而言，变化就是一切。最近的研究表明，手机不仅改变着我们的文化，也改变着我们的身体本身。

先说文化。手机与它的「父辈」固定电话的区别在于：你打过去，是谁接就是谁。这有几层含义。但最常见、也许永远改变了我们文化的一点，是「约会效应」。人们不再需要就何时何地见面订下确定的计划。20 年前，周五晚上出去玩得提前安排；而现在，一个夜生活可以在路上临时约成。

发短信也在改变人。在论文《短信的社交与心理影响透视》中，两位英国研究者区分了两类手机用户：「说的人」和「写的人」——偏爱语音胜过短信的，和偏爱短信胜过语音的。他们发现，手机的个体性和私密性让「写的人」有能力表达一种全新的外在性格。「写的人」往往会说，如果家人读到他们的短信会大吃一惊。

另一位科学家写到手机给肢体语言带来的变化。人们打电话时使用两种肢体语言：一种是「自在说话型」——头高高抬起、显得自信，聊个不停；另一种是「占位型」——这些人专注于自己，把别人隔在外面。

C 节 · 讲座一（第 16—19 题）

—— 多年来人们一直在跟邻居攀比。那何不真正试着跟邻居和睦相处呢？今天来和我们分享一些简单建议的，是贝蒂·王，她是《家庭圈》杂志的执行主编，讲的是如何应对那些讨人喜欢和不太讨人喜欢的邻居。早上好，贝蒂。
—— 大家早上好。
—— 首先你可能会问：为什么跟邻居保持良好关系很重要？你知道，家是你的庇护所，而你和邻居相处得如何，对你的健康、幸福和快乐有很大影响。所以，至少要和邻居建立良好、友善，或者至少礼貌的关系。
—— 搬进一个社区时，你应该建立关系。如果邻居没有主动来接触你，不要以为他们无礼或不友好。过几天，主动去自我介绍，因为我觉得一旦你跟他们成了朋友，以后预防问题就容易得多。或者请他们帮个忙，比如你去度假时需要他们帮你浇花、取邮件。彼此认识之后，这些都容易多了。
—— 是啊，邻居真的能帮上大忙，但当然也可能很烦人。比如，吵闹的音乐是最大的抱怨之一，我想，多数情况下，人们可能根本不知道自己在给邻居添麻烦。我觉得，如果你提醒一下邻居，他们会很乐意改正。但别一上来就叫警察。你可以这样说：「你知道吗，我睡眠很浅」，或者「我常头痛，能不能麻烦你在晚上或清早那几个小时把音乐调小一点？」或者想出一个对双方都管用的折中办法——一个双方都能接受的解决方案。
—— 还有一种很敏感的情况：难闻的气味。但你的邻居同样有权在自己家里舒舒服服地做她喜欢做的菜。你应该礼貌、理性地去跟他们沟通；如果不管用，你也可以去找物业，因为也许你们楼的通风系统出了问题。
—— 另外，本月的《家庭圈》提到了「人多力量大」，意思是有时候争取其他邻居的支持确实有帮助，但你得注意，别变成联合起来对付隔壁邻居。关于这个话题以及其他内容，可以参阅我们的杂志。

C 节 · 讲座二（第 20—22 题）

移动设备的普及带来了一些意想不到、甚至危险的后果。我们现在知道，移动通讯与分心驾驶的显著增加有关，导致人员受伤和死亡。

美国国家公路交通安全管理局报告称，今年所有致命车祸中有 18% 是驾驶分心造成的，共 3328 人死亡；造成人员受伤的事故中，有 42.1 万人受伤。一项调查显示，40% 的美国青少年说他们坐过车、而司机以危及他人安全的方式使用手机。在 18 至 20 岁、遭遇车祸并幸存的驾驶者中，11% 承认撞车时正在收发短信。

分心驾驶危及生命和财产，目前的伤亡水平是不可接受的。为解决这个问题，美国联邦通信委员会（FCC）正与行业安全组织和其他政府机构合作，向公众宣传分心驾驶的危险，并寻求识别和推动开发能够减少分心驾驶的创新技术。为协助这项工作并共享信息，我们建立了一个专门的网站。

目前，全国还没有禁止开车时发短信或使用无线电话的联邦法律，但一些州已通过法律，禁止开车时发短信或使用无线电话，或要求开车时必须免手使用无线电话。

父母应当给青少年驾驶者简单明确的指示：开车时不要使用无线设备。据美国蜂窝电信工业协会的说法，最简单的说法是：「在路上，就离开电话。」在新手司机拿到驾照之前，要跟他们讲清楚：目光离开路面哪怕只有几秒，也可能导致他人受伤甚至死亡。

孩子会模仿父母的行为。任何人都不该边发短信边开车。给孩子做个榜样；如果你需要发短信或打电话，就把车停到安全的地方。

了解信息并积极行动。阅读我们网站上的信息和资料。为自己和家庭制定关于分心驾驶的规则。告诉家人、朋友和你所属的组织「不分心驾驶」的重要性。把资料带到孩子的学校，请学校转达给学生和家长。

C 节 · 讲座三（第 23—25 题）

今年早些时候，我去了一趟英国和法国，去看法国的一些朋友。那是一趟很棒的旅行，我真的很喜欢。但有一件事让我印象深刻——我想任何人旅行时都会有同感——就是别的文化与我们的文化有多么不同。不只是不同，也有多么相似；不过我想，真正突出的是那些差异。

让我印象最深的事情之一，是对吸烟态度的差异。许多人都知道，欧洲的反吸烟情绪在增长。然而，我到英国和法国时，对这个问题有了新的看法。人们似乎在任何地方、任何场合都吸烟，尽管公共场所到处都有禁烟标志。

我在广播里好几次听到世界杯足球队里有一名球员吸烟。人们竟然说：「他不该留在队里，因为他给孩子树立了坏榜样。」我想，如果他们想给孩子找吸烟的坏榜样，那就到大街上、到地铁里去看看，或者干脆照照镜子——因为他们那么多人在非常不合适的场合吸烟。

我去伦敦一家餐厅，那里有自助餐。有一位英国女士手里拿着烟——点着的烟。她一边吐烟，一边把烟直接举在自助餐的食物上方。其实，后来我跟英国人聊起这事，他们也相当震惊，说这按英国的标准都算无礼。

这件事不只让我觉得欧洲人不好，反过来，它也对我对美国吸烟者的看法产生了正面影响。有很多美国吸烟者会宣称自己随时想抽就抽的权利，但他们一般会遵守规定。总体而言，他们确实会顾及不吸烟的人，所以这次在欧洲的经历让我对这类吸烟者多了几分尊重。

title: Model Test 7 · 综合训练
en:
Section A — Conversation One (Questions 1–4)

— Did you feel like you need more hours from the day? Well, Good Housekeeping magazine has some advice on how you can stop wasting time and get it all done, and here with the top 10 tips is Carolyn Forte. Hey Carolyn, good morning.
— Good morning, Hoda. Nice to be here.
— Your number one tip is bank online. Some people are afraid to do it, but you say it's something smart.
— Yeah, it is very safe, and we certainly recommend that you use your own bank's website. So go to the bank, talk to the consumer service representatives there. It's the best way to find out how safe it is and how easy.
— And how much time do you think you could save, Carolyn, by doing that?
— If you're making transfers or checking your statements, you can save up to an hour.
— The second tip is online grocers. Now that's really not for everyone, but you actually go grocery shopping online.
— That's exactly what you do. If you're the type of person that wants to read every label and look at every piece of fruit, it's probably not for you. But if you want to give up a little control, you can definitely save some time.
— And what's the good strategy if you decide to shop online?
— What I would suggest is do the staples online.
— What do they include?
— The brands that you use all the time, the paper products, the cleaning products, the cereals — get them online and go to the store for the meat and the produce.
— That's enlightening.

Section A — Conversation Two (Questions 5–8)

— Dan, did you want to see me?
— Oh, yes, Sue, please sit down. We need some help.
— What can I do?
— Look at this schedule. There are four conferences in April and there aren't enough representatives to cover all of them.

— I know, but you have studied management and merchandising, and we have openings for more managerial people. There is a good opportunity for you here.

— There's a conference in Seattle on the 18th of April. I want you to represent us.
— That's a big responsibility.
— You'll do very well, I'm pretty sure.
— Is there a lot to learn?
— There are a few things but they aren't difficult. There isn't much time left.
— Can I start now?
— There are some reports on the previous conferences and the files. You can study those.
— Can you give me any guidelines about etiquette in other countries?
— There are several overall guidelines that apply to international conferences.
— Then where can I find all the country-specific information?
— Usually you can call that country's embassy or consulate. Most of them have printed materials for business visitors, and there are also travel books available at public libraries. If you don't have enough time, you can also ask Sally, as she attended the conference there last time.
— Great. And will our company arrange for transportation?
— Yes, tell the travel department about what you think you'll need and they can make arrangements for you.
— Thank you. I'll give it my best shot.

Section B — Passage One (Questions 9–11)

Objects that are vibrating make sounds. Rhythmic sound vibrations produce sound waves which travel in every direction. The frequency of a sound is the number of waves that pass a given point each second. The more rapidly an object vibrates, the greater the frequency of sound it makes.

Frequency is measured in hertz; one hertz equals one sound wave per second. The frequency of sound determines the degree of highness or lowness of the sound. A high-pitched sound has a higher frequency than a low-pitched sound.

Humans hear sounds that have frequencies from about 20 hertz to 20,000 hertz. Sound with a frequency higher than 20,000 hertz is called ultrasound, which is too high-pitched for humans to hear. However, many animals can hear ultrasound.

Bats can hear higher sounds than any other animal. Some can hear up to 210,000 hertz. Bats send out lots of high-pitched squeaks and then listen to the echoes bouncing off things like insects. The shorter the time interval between a squeak and the echo, the closer they are to the insect. Using sound to find or see things is called echolocation.

Another animal that uses ultrasound is the dolphin. Dolphins can hear sounds up to about 150,000 hertz. Dolphins use sound waves to find food underwater. They make clicking sounds that hit whatever is around them and then bounce back to the dolphins. Dolphins can send as many as 2,000 clicks per second. Dolphins' ultrasound ability is so sensitive that they can detect small fish from 10 feet away.

Section B — Passage Two (Questions 12–15)

During the Christmas shopping rush in London, an interesting story was reported of a tramp who, apparently through no fault of his own, found himself locked in a well-known chain store late on Christmas Eve. No doubt the store was crowded with last-minute Christmas shoppers, and the staff were dead beat and longing to go home. Maybe all the proper security checks were made before the store was locked, and they left to enjoy the three-day holiday untroubled by customers desperate to get last-minute Christmas presents.

However funny that may be, our tramp found himself alone in the store and decided to make the best of it. There was food, drink, bedding and camping equipment, of which he made good use. There must also have been television sets and radios, though it was not reported if he took advantage of these things.

When the shop reopened, he was discovered in bed with a large number of empty bottles beside him. He seems to have been a man of good humor and calm character, as indeed tramps very commonly are. He gave in cheerfully enough to being taken away by the police.

Perhaps he had had a better Christmas than usual. He was sent to prison for seven days. The judge awarded no compensation to the chain store for the food and drink our tramp had consumed. They had, in his opinion, already received valuable free publicity from the coverage the story received in the newspapers and on television.

Section C — Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

As long as there has been crime, there have been ways to solve it. One of the oldest methods is interrogation, a method in which the police question people who might have committed the crime or who might have information about the crime. Interrogation can help the police to establish many basic facts, but modern techniques for solving crime include more complex scientific methods.

Let me talk first about a system often called crime hotlines. In some cases where law enforcement personnel have difficulty finding a criminal, they turn to private citizens for help in solving a crime. This system allows people to make a phone call or access a website and give information to the police anonymously. This can often be effective when people are afraid to give information in public. Sometimes a family member may have committed the crime and another family member finally decides to call the police and give the information they have.

Second, fingerprinting. Each person's fingerprint is unique. The ancient Chinese used fingerprints to sign legal papers. What better way to identify an individual? Yet it was only in the late 19th century that fingerprints were first used to identify criminals. A variety of scientific techniques makes it possible for fingerprints to be lifted from most surfaces.

A relatively new technique that crime fighters are now using is called psychological profiling. Criminal psychologists look at the crime and the way it was committed. Based on this information, they try to understand the personality and motivation of the person who committed the crime. Then they can focus their search on people who match this profile.

In some cases, private citizens are finding ways to solve crimes as well. With a little knowledge of electronics, anyone can put hidden cameras in a home or office. In the 1990s, as an example, there were some cases where nannies were accused of abusing the children they were paid to care for. Hidden cameras were used to prove the nanny's guilt. However, the technique is controversial because it involves issues of privacy.

Finally, let me discuss DNA, one of the most recent crime-solving techniques used. DNA is proving very effective. Each person, with the exception of identical twins, has a unique DNA coding system. So if criminals leave anything that can be tested at the scene of the crime, such as blood or hair, they can be identified. DNA was used to solve a crime for the first time in England in 1987. Since that time, it has become widely used and it is considered 99% accurate. DNA testing can also be used to prove that a person is innocent. Many prisoners have been released because DNA evidence proves that they did not commit the crime of which they were convicted.

Section C — Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

Thank you all for coming to my talk this evening. It's nice to see so many people in the audience. Building team spirit is always the focal point of what I have been trying to do as a manager.

When I first went to Crystal Palace, football players would finish training and then go straight home. There was no atmosphere, so we brought in a pool table and fruit machines. When football players choose to spend time together, it generates a better atmosphere.

The team spirit is very important, but I don't believe in trying to motivate the team as a team. I try to motivate them as individuals. So I don't give team talks. I speak to the players individually and I try not to put too much pressure on them. I believe that football players perform best when they are relaxed. If they are too tense, I can guarantee they won't play well in a game.

I also believe in giving people autonomy. I like all the people who work for me to be autonomous; therefore I very rarely interfere. I feel people should be judged on their results. If they prove incompetent, then I'm incompetent if I keep on employing them. It's like that with the team.

I get criticized for not interfering during a game and making more substitutions, but I feel if I've chosen these 11 players to get a result, then I should leave them alone to get on with it. If I'm dropping a player from the team, I don't feel I have to explain it to them. If they want to discuss it, I'll say come back and talk about it in a couple of days' time. But I don't try to re-motivate them. It's up to them to have the character to fight back.

I'm a great believer that almost everything you achieve in life is down to your attitude. If I have a football player who is magnificently gifted but has a bad attitude, I won't waste my time on him.

Section C — Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

Listening is one of the first things we learn to do and one of the things we do most. The average person spends 9% of their daily communication time writing, 16% reading, 30% speaking and 40% listening. Students spend most of their school time listening — up to 60%, according to some studies.

Yet despite its importance, we usually take our ability to listen for granted. As we have already said, though, listening isn't easy. The fact is we have different listening styles for different occasions. How successful we are as listeners may depend in part on choosing the right listening style for the situation.

Perhaps the most basic listening style is appreciative listening. We listen appreciatively when we enjoy music, a bird's song or the murmur of a brook.

We need a different style, one called discriminative listening, when we want to single out one particular sound from a noisy environment. You discriminate, for example, when you listen for a friend's voice in a crowded room.

We use a third style of listening, comprehensive listening, when we want to understand. When we listen to directions or instructions, we are using this style.

The fourth listening style is more complex: therapeutic listening. The style, practiced by counselors, psychiatrists and good friends, encourages people to talk freely without fear of embarrassment. Friends act as our sounding boards when we just want someone to listen. The therapeutic listener, in conversation with a troubled friend, accepts what he says, tries hard to understand, and above all, makes no judgment.

The fifth style, critical listening, is the one we will examine most closely. Critical listeners are the most active of all listeners, because they are working hard to decide whether what someone else says makes sense. Critical listeners evaluate what they hear and decide if another person's message is logical, worthwhile, or has value. We need to be critical listeners when someone wants us to buy some things, vote a certain way, or support a particular idea. We also need to be critical listeners in school, where listening and thinking are almost identical.

A 节 · 对话一（第 1—4 题）

—— 你是不是觉得一天需要更多小时？《好管家》杂志给了一些建议，教你怎么不再浪费时间、把事都做完。今天带来「十大妙招」的是卡罗琳·福特。嘿，卡罗琳，早上好。
—— 早上好，霍达。很高兴来这儿。
—— 你的第一招是「网上办银行业务」。有些人不敢这么做，但你说这很聪明。
—— 对，这非常安全，我们当然建议你使用自己银行的网站。所以去一趟银行，跟那里的客服代表谈谈，这是了解它有多安全、多方便的最好办法。
—— 卡罗琳，你觉得这样做能省多少时间？
—— 如果你要转账或者查对账单，最多能省一个小时。
—— 第二招是网上买菜。这确实不适合所有人，但你真的会在网上买食品杂货？
—— 正是如此。如果你是那种要看每一个标签、看每一个水果的人，这可能不适合你。但如果你愿意放弃一点掌控权，肯定能省下一些时间。
—— 那如果决定网上购物，有什么好策略？
—— 我的建议是：耐用品在网上买。
—— 都包括什么？
—— 你一直用的品牌、纸制品、清洁用品、麦片——这些在网上买，肉和生鲜蔬果去店里买。
—— 真是让人开窍。

—— 哦，是的，苏，请坐。我们需要帮手。

B 节 · 篇章一（第 9—11 题）

振动的物体发出声音。有节奏的声振动产生向各个方向传播的声波。声音的频率是每秒通过某一点的波的数量。物体振动得越快，它发出声音的频率就越高。

频率以赫兹计量，1 赫兹等于每秒一个声波。声音的频率决定音调的高低。高音调的频率高于低音调。

人耳能听到频率约 20 赫兹到 20000 赫兹的声音。频率高于 20000 赫兹的声音叫超声，音调太高，人耳听不到。不过，许多动物能听到超声。

蝙蝠能听到比其他任何动物都高的声音，有些能听到高达 21 万赫兹。蝙蝠发出大量高音尖叫，然后听这些声音从昆虫等物体上反射回来的回声。尖叫与回声之间的时间间隔越短，它们离昆虫就越近。用声音来发现或「看见」物体，叫做回声定位。

另一种使用超声的动物是海豚。海豚能听到约 15 万赫兹的声音。海豚利用声波在水下寻找食物。它们发出咔嗒声，声音碰到周围物体后反弹回海豚。海豚每秒能发出多达 2000 次咔嗒声。海豚的超声能力极其灵敏，能在 10 英尺外发现小鱼。

B 节 · 篇章二（第 12—15 题）

在伦敦圣诞购物潮中，报道了一个有趣的故事：一名流浪汉显然并非自己的过错，在平安夜很晚的时候发现自己被锁在一家知名连锁店里。毫无疑问，店里挤满了赶着买最后一批圣诞礼物的顾客，员工们累得要命，急着回家。也许在锁门前做了所有该做的安全检查，然后他们就去享受三天假期，不再被那些拼命想买到最后一份圣诞礼物的顾客打扰。

不管这事多好笑，我们的流浪汉发现自己独自待在店里，便决定尽量利用一下。那里有食物、饮料、床上用品和露营装备，他都好好用上了。店里肯定还有电视和收音机，不过没有报道他是否用了这些东西。

店重新开门时，人们发现他躺在床上，旁边堆着一大堆空瓶子。他似乎是个脾气好、性格沉稳的人——流浪汉确实常常如此。他很痛快地跟着警察走了。

也许他这个圣诞节比往常过得好。他被判入狱七天。法官没有判连锁店获得流浪汉所消费的食物和饮料的赔偿。在他看来，这家店已经从报纸和电视对此事的报道中获得了宝贵的免费宣传。

C 节 · 讲座一（第 16—19 题）

自从有了犯罪，就有了破案的办法。最古老的方法之一是审讯，即警察询问可能实施了犯罪、或可能掌握犯罪信息的人。审讯能帮警察确定许多基本事实，但现代破案技术还包括更复杂的科学方法。

先说一种常被称为「犯罪热线」的系统。在执法人员难以找到罪犯的情况下，他们有时会求助于普通公民协助破案。这一系统允许人们打电话或访问网站，匿名向警方提供信息。当人们害怕公开提供信息时，这往往很有效。有时是家庭成员犯了罪，而另一个家庭成员最终决定报警并提供所知信息。

第二，指纹。每个人的指纹都是独一无二的。古代中国人用指纹来签署法律文书。还有什么比这更好的识别个人的方法？然而，指纹直到 19 世纪末才首次被用于识别罪犯。各种科学手段使指纹几乎可以从任何表面提取。

犯罪打击者现在使用的一种较新技术叫「心理侧写」。犯罪心理学家研究犯罪以及作案方式，据此设法了解犯罪者的人格和动机，然后集中搜查符合这一侧写的人。

在某些情况下，普通公民也在想办法破案。只要懂一点电子知识，任何人都可以在家里或办公室安装隐蔽摄像头。例如 20 世纪 90 年代，有些案件中的保姆被指控虐待受托照顾的孩子，隐蔽摄像头被用来证明保姆有罪。不过，这种技术有争议，因为它涉及隐私问题。

最后，我谈谈 DNA——目前使用的最新破案技术之一。DNA 被证明非常有效。除同卵双胞胎外，每个人的 DNA 编码系统都是独一无二的。所以如果罪犯在犯罪现场留下了可供检测的东西，比如血液或头发，就能被识别出来。1987 年，DNA 首次在英国用于破案。此后它被广泛使用，被认为有 99% 的准确率。DNA 检测也可以用来证明一个人无罪。许多囚犯因为 DNA 证据证明他们没有犯下被判定的罪行而获释。

C 节 · 讲座二（第 20—22 题）

感谢大家今晚来听我的讲座，很高兴看到这么多听众。培养团队精神，一直是我作为主教练努力的重点。

我刚到水晶宫时，球员训练一结束就直接回家，毫无气氛。于是我们添置了一张台球桌和几台老虎机。当球员们愿意待在一起时，气氛就会更好。

团队精神非常重要，但我不主张把球队当成一个整体去激励。我试着以个人的方式去激励他们，所以我不做全队讲话。我跟球员单独交流，尽量不给他们太大压力。我相信球员在放松的时候表现最好。如果他们太紧张，我敢保证他们在比赛中踢不好。

我也主张给人自主权。我希望为我工作的所有人都能自主，因此我很少干预。我认为应当按结果来评价人。如果他们被证明无能，那我继续雇他们就是我的无能。带球队也是如此。

有人批评我在比赛中不干预、不更多换人，但我觉得既然我选了这 11 名球员去争取结果，就该让他们自己去踢。如果我把某名球员从阵容中拿掉，我并不觉得非得向他解释。如果他想谈，我会说：过两天再来谈。但我不会去重新激励他。能不能拿出性格来反击，得靠他自己。

我深信，人生中几乎一切成就都取决于你的态度。如果我有一名天赋极高但态度很差的球员，我不会在他身上浪费时间。

C 节 · 讲座三（第 23—25 题）

倾听是我们最早学会的事情之一，也是我们做得最多的事情之一。普通人每天的沟通时间里，9% 用于写、16% 用于读、30% 用于说、40% 用于听。有些研究显示，学生上学期间大部分时间都在听——高达 60%。

然而，尽管倾听如此重要，我们通常把自己的倾听能力视为理所当然。正如我们已经说过的，倾听并不容易。事实是，不同场合我们有不同的倾听方式。我们作为倾听者有多成功，部分取决于是否针对情境选择了正确的倾听风格。

也许最基本的倾听方式是「欣赏式倾听」。我们在欣赏音乐、鸟鸣或溪水潺潺时，就是在欣赏式地听。

我们需要另一种方式，叫「辨别式倾听」，用于从嘈杂环境中分辨出某一个特定的声音。例如，在拥挤的房间里分辨出朋友的声音，你就在进行辨别式倾听。

第三种方式是「理解式倾听」，用于我们想要弄懂的时候。听指路或听指令时，我们用的就是这种方式。

第四种倾听方式更复杂：「治疗式倾听」。咨询师、精神科医生和好朋友会用这种方式，它鼓励人们畅所欲言而不必担心尴尬。当我们只想有人听自己说话时，朋友就是我们的「回音板」。治疗式倾听者与心事重重的朋友交谈时，接受对方所说的话，努力去理解，最重要的是不作评判。

第五种方式「批判式倾听」，是我们将最仔细考察的一种。批判式倾听者是一切倾听者中最积极的，因为他们在努力判断别人说的话是否讲得通。批判式倾听者评估所听到的内容，判断对方的信息是否合乎逻辑、是否有价值。当有人想让我们买东西、按某种方式投票或支持某个观点时，我们需要做批判式倾听者。在学校里我们也需要批判式倾听，因为在那里听和思考几乎是同一件事。

title: Model Test 8 · 综合训练
en:
Section A — Conversation One (Questions 1–4)

— We've all heard the saying "laughter is the best medicine." How important is it to our health, Dr. Burke?
— This saying has been scientifically proven. A year-long study of heart attack victims, done at the Oakhurst Health Research Institute in California, found that of those patients who spent half an hour a day watching comedy videos, 10% had a second heart attack, whereas 30% of those who did not watch had a second attack.
— Wow, laughter is really a good medicine for patients. Can you give us another example?
— Sure. Norman Cousins, editor of the Saturday Review, learned this during a battle with an illness. He discovered that his condition improved when he enjoyed himself and watched funny movies.
— You said Norman learned this. Do we have to learn to laugh?
— Not necessarily, since laughing is something people can do. Sitting down costs no money and requires no special exercise, equipment or skill. It's the perfect workout for anyone who doesn't have the time or desire to participate in a regular fitness program.
— Oh, do you have such a program to offer to the general public?
— Yes, we do. It's called the "Smile Time-Out." You take a deep breath, smile, exhale and say "ah" while visualizing all your muscles and cells smiling. Then add to that a memory of a time you felt really good and laughed and laughed.
— What about the situation in which you aren't in the mood to laugh?
— Even when you fake a smile or laugh, you get the same psychological benefits as when it's the real thing. Because your mind is smart, but your body is stupid and can't tell the difference.

Section A — Conversation Two (Questions 5–8)

— Time to eat.
— Coming. I'm starving.
— Oh yuck, what's that?
— Ah, now don't complain.
— But what is it, and where is Mom?
— Now, Mom put me in charge of dinner because she's not feeling well tonight.
— But what is it? And that smell.
— It's pizza. I just followed an old family recipe here and —
— Let me see that. Oh, Dad, you're missing a page.
— Oh, uh, well, I couldn't find the second page of the recipe, but don't worry, I have plenty of experience around the house — plenty of experience in cooking.
— That's not what Mom says.
— Well, wait, wait, here, let me try a piece first. Here, let me cool this off here. Oh yeah, oh, this is great stuff.
— Yeah, right.
— Why are you making faces?
— Well, it's just a little rich for me, that's all.
— Let me try it, Dad. Uh, Dad, you put a little too much salt in it, and besides, it's burned. And what's that?
— Oh, well, that's just part of my own adaptation to the recipe. I added some pumpkin.
— Oh, not another one of your surprises. Pumpkin doesn't go on pizza.
— Well, okay, so what do we do now?
— Well, how about some cold cereal? You can't mess up on that, Dad.
— Oh, I love cereal.

Section B — Passage One (Questions 9–12)

Yuppies are young people who earn a lot of money and live in a style that is too expensive for most people. If you are invited to a yuppie dinner party, don't be surprised if you are offered freshly cooked insects as the first course. While the idea of eating fried insects fills most of us with horror, insect eating is becoming highly fashionable.

For example, in the media industry, successful executives are often seen to eat fried or boiled insects from time to time while working at their desks. These safe-to-eat insects can be found and ordered on the internet, and young people are logging on to exotic food websites and ordering samples of prepared insects to serve at their dinner parties.

Although the idea of eating insects is probably disgusting to most of us, few people would claim that pigs, chickens, and some kinds of seafood we often eat are examples of great beauty. One day, insects could be marketed and sold as a food item in supermarkets. According to their fans, they are not only high in protein and low in fat, but also very tasty. But until our attitudes to food change fundamentally, it seems that insect eaters will remain a select few.

Section B — Passage Two (Questions 13–15)

Many people dislike walking into the bank, standing in long lines and running out of checks. They are dissatisfied with their bank's limited hours, too. They want to do some banking at night and on weekends.

For such people, their problems may soon be over. Before long, they may be able to do their banking from the comfort of their own home, any hour of the day, any day of the week. Many banks are preparing online branches or internet offices, which mean that people will be able to take care of much of their banking business through their home computers. This process is called interactive banking.

At these online branches, customers will be able to view all their accounts, move money between their accounts, apply for a loan and get current information on products such as credit cards. Customers will also be able to pay their bills electronically and even email questions to the bank.

Banks are creating online services for several reasons. One reason is that banks must compete for customers, who will switch to another bank if they are dissatisfied with the service they receive. The convenience of online banking appeals to the kind of customer banks most want to keep — that is, people who are young, well educated and have good incomes. Banks also want to take advantage of modern technology since they have moved into the 21st century.

Section C — Lecture One (Questions 16–19)

The Harvard Study of Adult Development may be the longest study of adult life that's ever been done. For 75 years, we've tracked the lives of 724 men year after year to find out one thing: what keeps us healthy and happy as we go through life?

To get the clearest picture of these lives, we don't just send them questionnaires. We interview them in their living rooms, we get their medical records from their doctors, we draw their blood, we scan their brains, and we talk to their children. We videotape them talking with their families about their deepest concerns.

So what have we learned? Well, the lessons aren't about wealth or fame or working harder and harder. The clearest message that we get from this 75-year study is this: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.

We've learned three big lessons about relationships. The first is that social connections are really good for us. People who are more socially connected to family, to friends, to community are happier, they're physically healthier, and they live longer than people who are less well connected. And the experience of loneliness turns out to be bad. People who are more isolated than they want to be from others find that they are less happy, their health declines earlier in midlife. And we know that you can be lonely in a crowd and you can be lonely in a marriage.

So the second big lesson that we learned is that it's not just the number of friends you have, and it's not whether or not you're in a committed relationship, but it's the quality of your close relationships that matters. High-conflict marriages, for example, without much affection, turn out to be very bad for our health — perhaps worse than getting divorced. And good close relationships seem to shelter us from some of the hardship of getting old. Our most happily partnered men and women reported, in their eighties, that on the days when they had more physical pain, their mood stayed just as happy.

And the third big lesson that we learned about relationships and our health is that good relationships don't just protect our bodies, they protect our brains. And those good relationships, they don't have to be smooth all the time. Some of the couples in their eighties or nineties could quarrel with each other day in and day out, but as long as they felt that they could really count on the other when the going got tough, those quarrels didn't do huge harm on their memories.

So this message that good close relationships are good for our health and well-being — this is wisdom that's as old as the hills.

Section C — Lecture Two (Questions 20–22)

As we all know, banks do charge fees of two dollars or three dollars at a time to non-customers accessing their cash. And these fees add up in a big way, totaling 7.1 billion dollars last year alone. According to a recent survey conducted by Ally Bank, 77% of Americans feel that it's not okay for banks to charge ATM fees. More than half — 56% — of those surveyed said that the proper fee for an ATM transaction is zero dollars. It's your money you're accessing, after all, the thinking goes.

Everyone can avoid these fees by using only affiliated ATMs, but quite obviously plenty of consumers find it necessary from time to time to use another bank's machine, even if doing so incurs a fee.

But what if there was another way? What if there was an ATM that anyone could use that never charged fees? There is one such ATM actually, and there could be more to come.

A company called Free ATMs NYC operates an ATM at a music venue called the Knitting Factory in Brooklyn. All users are welcome to make withdrawals entirely fee-free. While the transaction is occurring, a 15-inch video screen above the ATM shows an advertisement. When the transaction is complete, the customer gets a receipt along with a little more advertising or marketing in the form of a coupon, good for a discount to a local business, perhaps a nearby restaurant. Even with the ads, the transaction is done in roughly the same time it takes to get money from any other ATM.

The customer could switch to a bank that doesn't charge such fees, and by some indication, millions of consumers are doing just that.

Free ATMs NYC is the brainchild of a 25-year-old entrepreneur named Clinton Townsend. The company's homepage says that it is aggressively rolling out a portfolio of free ATMs throughout New York City. But so far, there's just the one fee-free machine in Brooklyn — and only one throughout all of New York City and the US, for that matter.

Will the idea catch on? With no-fee ATMs popping up left and right, the concept would surely be popular with consumers. As mentioned earlier, most people think that the proper fee for an ATM transaction is no fee at all, and that's what Free ATMs NYC delivers.

Section C — Lecture Three (Questions 23–25)

Ever since McDonald's adopted a strategy in 2003 that focuses on improving existing restaurants and adding new menu items, the burger giant has been globally successful. Even during the latest economic downturn, its growth is not slow, and in the third quarter its revenue and profit exceeded analysts' expectations. McDonald's shares are up more than 63% in the last three years, having closed Monday at 98 dollars and 48 cents, and many analysts expect its stock to break 100 dollars soon. The company beat Wall Street again last week when it posted its 103rd month of positive global same-store sales.

So what's McDonald's secret of success? For one thing, it is relying heavily on emerging markets such as China for new restaurant growth. The company last week reported that its Asia-Pacific, Middle East and Africa divisions posted the strongest same-store sales growth last month of all its business units, with sales up 8.1% from the year before.

The company cited compelling customer conveniences as one of the growth drivers at work. One of those conveniences is adding dessert windows on the exterior of existing restaurants, where pedestrians can order an ice cream cone instead of being in line inside the restaurant. Another is delivering food by bicycle in countries like China, Egypt and South Korea.

All over the world, the company is updating its restaurants, modernizing the decoration and adding such facilities as free Wi-Fi and flat-screen televisions. It has also extended restaurant hours to attract customers who don't dine during the traditional workday, and added double-lane drive-thrus to get more customers through the line more quickly.

In the US, McDonald's is offering snack items such as chicken wraps and small desserts throughout most of the day. That allows the chain to attract customers during the otherwise slow periods between breakfast, lunch and dinner. The company also has added a lot of new menu items that are priced relatively high, low and in between, to appeal to a broad range of consumers. That enables the chain to appeal to everyone from the traditional fast-food addict who loves burgers, to salad-chomping moms, to the employee on the go who wants to grab a bowl of porridge for breakfast. Meanwhile, the high-margin items such as strawberry lemonade, fruit smoothies and fancy coffee drinks have protected profits by offsetting cheaper items like one-dollar hamburgers.

Questions

1. What did the year-long study of heart attack victims find?
2. What is Norman's example meant to prove?
3. What is the so-called "Smile Time-Out"?
4. What can we learn about smiling or laughing, according to Dr. Burke?
5. What problem does the girl notice about her father's cooking?
6. How does the girl know her father doesn't like the pizza he prepared?
7. What is the man's own adaptation to the recipe?
8. What do they end up doing for their supper?
9. Why does the speaker say we might be surprised at the yuppie dinner party?
10. Where can people order the unusual food mentioned by the speaker?
11. Why are some yuppies attracted by the unusual food?
12. What does the speaker say about the future of this type of unusual food?
13. What is one of the reasons for people's dissatisfaction with traditional banks?
14. What kind of customer does online banking most appeal to?
15. Why do banks create online services, according to the passage?
16. What did the Harvard Study of Adult Development try to find out?
17. What is the study's conclusion about loneliness?
18. What is the most important for a relationship, according to the second lesson?
19. Why don't small quarrels among old couples affect their relationship?
20. What can we conclude from the survey conducted by Ally Bank?
21. What can the customer get from Free ATMs NYC?
22. How many fee-free ATMs can we find in New York City?
23. How did McDonald's shares perform in the last three years?
24. What compelling customer conveniences does McDonald's bring to customers?
25. What did McDonald's do to appeal to a broad range of consumers?
zh:
A 节 · 对话一（第 1—4 题）

—— 我们都听过「笑是最好的良药」这句话。伯克博士，笑对我们的健康有多重要？
—— 这句话已经被科学证实了。加州奥克赫斯特健康研究所对心脏病发作患者做了一项为期一年的研究，发现每天看半小时喜剧视频的病人中，有 10% 再次发作；而不看的人中有 30% 再次发作。
—— 哇，笑对病人真是好药。能再举一个例子吗？
—— 当然。《星期六评论》的编辑诺曼·考辛斯在与疾病抗争时学到了这一点。他发现，当他让自己开心、看搞笑电影时，病情会好转。
—— 你说诺曼「学到」了这一点。我们得学着去笑吗？
—— 不一定，因为笑是人本来就会做的事。坐下来不花钱，也不需要特别的运动、器械或技巧。对任何没有时间或不打算参加常规健身计划的人来说，这是最完美的锻炼。
—— 哦，你们有没有向大众提供这样的方案？
—— 有，叫「微笑暂停」。你深吸一口气、微笑、呼气，同时说「啊」，并想象自己所有的肌肉和细胞都在微笑。然后再加进一段你曾经感觉很好、笑个不停的回忆。
—— 那如果你没心情笑呢？
—— 即便你假装微笑或假笑，得到的心理益处也和真笑一样。因为你的大脑很聪明，但你的身体很笨，分辨不出差别。

A 节 · 对话二（第 5—8 题）

—— 吃饭啦。
—— 来了，我饿死了。
—— 咦，那是什么？
—— 哎，别抱怨。
—— 可那是什么呀？妈妈呢？
—— 妈妈今晚不舒服，让我负责做晚饭。
—— 可这到底是什么？还有那股味道。
—— 是披萨，我照着家里的一份老菜谱做的，然后——
—— 让我看看。哦，爸爸，你少了一页。
—— 哦，呃，我找不到菜谱的第二页了，但别担心，我在家里经验丰富——做饭经验丰富。
—— 妈妈可不是这么说的。
—— 那等等，等等，我先尝一块。来，我把它吹凉一下。哦对，哦，这东西太棒了。
—— 是啊，是啊。
—— 你怎么做鬼脸了？
—— 嗯，就是对我来说有点太腻了，就这样。
—— 爸爸，我尝尝。呃，爸爸，你盐放多了一点，而且它还糊了。那又是什么？
—— 哦，那只是我自己对菜谱的一点改良，我加了点南瓜。
—— 哦，你又来这一套惊喜。南瓜可不能放在披萨上。
—— 好吧，那我们现在怎么办？
—— 要不吃点冷麦片？这个你可搞不砸，爸爸。
—— 哦，我爱麦片。

B 节 · 篇章一（第 9—12 题）

雅皮士是挣很多钱、过着对大多数人来说过于昂贵的生活方式的年轻人。如果你被邀请参加雅皮士的晚宴，第一道菜端上刚做好的昆虫时，别吃惊。虽然「吃油炸昆虫」这个念头让大多数人恐惧，但吃昆虫正变得非常时髦。

例如，在传媒业，人们常看到成功的高管在办公桌前工作时不时吃点油炸或水煮的昆虫。这些可安全食用的昆虫可以在网上找到并订购，年轻人登录异国食品网站，订购加工好的昆虫样品，在晚宴上端出来。

虽然吃昆虫的念头对我们大多数人来说大概很恶心，但很少有人会说我们常吃的猪、鸡和某些海鲜是美的典范。有一天，昆虫可能会作为食品在超市上架销售。据其拥趸说，它们不仅高蛋白、低脂肪，而且非常美味。但在我们对食物的态度发生根本改变之前，吃昆虫的人看来仍只是少数。

B 节 · 篇章二（第 13—15 题）

许多人不喜欢走进银行、排长队、支票用完。他们也对银行有限的营业时间不满，希望能在晚上和周末办一些银行业务。

对这些人来说，问题可能很快就能解决。不久之后，他们或许就能在自己舒适的家里、一周七天、一天二十四小时随时办理银行业务。许多银行正在筹建网上分行或网络办事处，这意味着人们可以通过家用电脑处理大部分银行业务。这一过程叫做「互动银行」。

在这些网上分行，客户可以查看自己所有账户、在账户间转账、申请贷款，并获取信用卡等产品的最新信息。客户还可以电子支付账单，甚至给银行发电子邮件提问。

银行开设网上服务有几个原因。原因之一是银行必须争夺客户——如果对服务不满，客户就会换到别的银行。网上银行的便利吸引的正是银行最想留住的客户——年轻、受过良好教育、收入不错的人。同时，进入 21 世纪后，银行也想利用现代技术。

C 节 · 讲座一（第 16—19 题）

哈佛成人发展研究可能是有史以来时间最长的成人生活研究。75 年来，我们年复一年地追踪 724 名男性的生活，只为弄清一件事：是什么让我们在一生中保持健康和快乐？

为了最清楚地了解这些人的生活，我们不只是发问卷。我们去他们家客厅访谈，从医生那里调取病历，抽血、扫描大脑，还跟他们的孩子交谈。我们用录像记录他们与家人谈论内心最深的忧虑。

那我们学到了什么？这些经验与财富、名望或越来越拼命地工作无关。这项 75 年研究给我们的最清晰的启示是：良好的人际关系让我们更快乐、更健康。

关于人际关系，我们学到三大经验。第一，社会联系确实对我们有益。与家人、朋友、社区联系更紧密的人更快乐、身体更健康，也比联系较少的人活得更久。而孤独的体验则是有害的。那些比自己所愿更孤立的人发现，自己不那么快乐，健康在中年更早衰退。我们也知道，你可以在人群里孤独，也可以在婚姻里孤独。

第二大经验是：关键不在于你有多少朋友，也不在于你是否处于一段承诺的关系中，而在于你亲密关系的质量。例如，缺乏感情、冲突激烈的婚姻对我们的健康非常有害，也许比离婚更糟。而良好亲密的关系似乎能为我们遮挡年老带来的部分艰难。我们那些伴侣关系最幸福的男女在八十多岁时表示，在身体更疼痛的日子里，他们的心情依然同样快乐。

关于人际关系与健康的第三大经验是：良好的人际关系不只保护我们的身体，也保护我们的大脑。而且这些良好关系不必时时平顺。有些八九十岁的夫妻天天拌嘴，但只要他们觉得自己在艰难时刻确实可以依靠对方，那些争吵对他们的记忆力并没有造成大的损害。

所以，「良好的亲密关系有益于我们的健康和幸福」这个信息，其实是古老得不能再古老的智慧。

C 节 · 讲座二（第 20—22 题）

众所周知，非本行客户取现时，银行确实每次收取两到三美元的手续费。这些费用累积起来数额惊人，仅去年一年就达 71 亿美元。据 Ally 银行最近的一项调查，77% 的美国人认为银行收取 ATM 手续费不妥。受访者中超过一半（56%）表示，ATM 交易的合理费用是零美元。毕竟，取的是你自己的钱——人们这么想。

只要只使用本行的 ATM，人人都能避开这些费用，但很明显，不少消费者时不时不得不用别家银行的机器，即使要付手续费。

但如果有别的办法呢？如果有一台任何人都能用、且从不收费的 ATM 呢？其实就有这样一台，而且可能会有更多。

一家名为「纽约免费 ATM」的公司在布鲁克林一个叫「针织厂」的音乐场地运营着一台 ATM。所有用户都可以完全免费取款。交易进行时，ATM 上方一块 15 英寸的屏幕播放广告；交易完成后，客户拿到凭条，同时还有一点广告或营销——以优惠券的形式，可在本地商家（也许是附近的餐厅）打折。即便有广告，交易耗时也与其他 ATM 取钱大致相同。

客户本可以换到不收这类费用的银行，而从某些迹象看，数百万消费者正是这么做的。

「纽约免费 ATM」是 25 岁创业者克林顿·汤森的点子。公司主页称，正大举在纽约全市铺开免费 ATM 组合。但到目前为止，布鲁克林只有那一台免费机器——就整个纽约市乃至全美而言，也只有这一台。

这个想法会流行起来吗？随着免费 ATM 到处出现，这个概念肯定会受消费者欢迎。如前所述，多数人认为 ATM 交易的合理费用就是完全不收费，而这正是「纽约免费 ATM」所提供的。

C 节 · 讲座三（第 23—25 题）

自从麦当劳 2003 年采取以改善现有餐厅、增加新菜单项目为重点的战略以来，这家汉堡巨头在全球一直很成功。即便在最近的经济低迷期，它的增长也不慢，第三季度营收和利润都超出分析师预期。过去三年麦当劳股价上涨逾 63%，周一收于 98.48 美元，许多分析师预计其股价很快会突破 100 美元。上周公司又跑赢华尔街，公布了全球同店销售连续第 103 个月正增长。

那麦当劳成功的秘诀是什么？一方面，它严重依赖中国等新兴市场来开设新餐厅。公司上周报告称，亚太、中东和非洲部门上月同店销售增长在所有业务单元中最强，销售额同比增长 8.1%。

公司把「令人心动的顾客便利」列为增长驱动因素之一。其中一项便利是在现有餐厅外墙增设甜品窗口，行人可以直接买一个冰淇淋蛋筒，不必进店排队。另一项是在中国、埃及、韩国等国家用自行车送餐。

在世界各地，公司都在翻新餐厅、更新装修，并增加免费 Wi-Fi 和平板电视等设施。它还延长营业时间以吸引不在传统工作时段用餐的顾客，并增设双车道得来速，让更多顾客更快通过。

在美国，麦当劳在一天中大部分时段提供鸡肉卷、小甜点等小食，这让连锁店能在早餐、午餐、晚餐之间的淡时段吸引顾客。公司还增加了许多价格较高、较低和居中的新菜单项目，以吸引广泛消费者。这使连锁店既能吸引热爱汉堡的传统快餐迷，也能吸引吃沙拉的妈妈们，还能吸引想抓一碗粥当早餐的上班族。同时，草莓柠檬水、水果冰沙和花式咖啡等高毛利产品，通过抵销一美元汉堡等低价产品，保护了利润。
